VII.1 — DEATH
You will not experience your death. Not as consolation — as
grammar: every experience you have is one you are having, so
there is no final one that arrives knowing it is final, and no ex‐
perience of afterward against which the difference could be
noticed. That keeps nobody here. It moves the event. Your
death is not something that happens to you; it is something
that happens to everyone else, and they are the ones who
have to be in the room afterward. The Ground continues, and
the Ground continuing is not you continuing: it cannot be ad‐
dressed, and nothing in it is having your experience. What
comes after is not one thing waiting to be named. Many states
are realizable; a plenum with a single sequel in it would not
be a plenum, and naming yours is the one move its structure
forbids. The not-knowing is about which, not about whether —
and what is realizable is realizable the way the Ground contin‐
ues: plural, actual, and not addressed to you. What you feel
when someone is gone is not a mistake about metaphysics. A
place where a world was happening is not happening, and the
people who were standing in it are still standing.
Two dreads wearing one word
Everything after this depends on a separation that most treat‐
ments of death never make, and the failure to make it is why
so many of them feel like sleight of hand even when every
step is sound.
Afraid to die names two fears. The first is of the void: of not
being, of the lights going out, of a nothing that is somehow
undergone. The second is of loss: of the people gone from the

world, of the unfinished sentence, of a house with the wrong
number of people in it. They arrive together and they share a
vocabulary, and they are not the same fear, and — the part
that matters — they do not have the same kind of answer.
One of them dissolves under inspection. The other does not
dissolve under anything, and this book will not pretend other‐
wise.
A treatment that takes them as one fear must either answer
both or neither. Answering both is what consolation is: it dis‐
solves the void and then applies the same solvent to the loss,
and a reader who has actually lost someone recognises the
trick immediately, because the second thing was not a confu‐
sion and cannot be argued out of them. Answering neither is
the shrug — nobody knows, be brave — and the shrug is what
the  reader  was  already  doing  before  they  opened  a  book
about it.
The separation is the whole of the method here. The first fear
gets an answer. The second gets accuracy, which is a different
thing and worth more than it sounds.
The one that dissolves, and the reason it has
never worked
Epicurus  made  the  argument,  and  he  made  it  in  a  form
nobody has improved: death is nothing to us, because while
we exist death is not present, and when death is present we
do not exist. So it is nothing to the living and nothing to the
dead.1 Lucretius,  working  the  same  ground  two  centuries
later, added the mirror that turns the argument from a defini‐
tion into a picture: an eternity elapsed before you, and it did
not trouble you. Nature holds up the time before your birth as

a specimen of the time after your death, and asks what in it
looks frightening.2
The argument is valid. It has convinced almost nobody, ever,
and the standard explanation for that — that people are irra‐
tional about death — is the laziest available and is wrong.
Thomas Nagel gave the serious objection in 1970, and it is the
best thing written against Epicurus in the modern period.3
Epicurus assumes that a misfortune requires a subject who is
present to undergo it. Nagel denies it. A man betrayed behind
his back and never told is wronged; a life cut short is deprived
of what it would have contained; the badness of death is not a
state anybody is in, it is a subtraction, and subtractions do
not require a sufferer standing in them to be real. This is why
the symmetry with prenatal time fails: the time before your
birth deprived you of nothing, because you would not have
had it anyway, and the time after your death takes what you
would otherwise have had.
Nagel is right against Epicurus. And the two of them, arguing,
share a premise this book does not hold.
Both are asking whether death is bad for the one who dies.
Epicurus answers no, on the grounds that there is no one for
it to be bad for; Nagel answers yes, on the grounds that the
for survives the absence of the sufferer. Neither questions the
preposition. Both keep a recipient in the sentence, and the en‐
tire dispute is about how much weight that recipient can bear
while missing.
Our claim is one step earlier and is not an evaluation at all.
There is no position at which the question is asked. Not
a position that finds the answer bad, not one that finds it neut‐
ral, not one that fails to find anything: no position. The first

paragraph of this chapter is the whole of it, and it is grammar
rather than metaphysics — a fact about where experience can
be indexed from, which was established in Book I on the first
page and has been load-bearing since.4
Which also explains the failure of Epicurus’s argument to con‐
sole anyone, and the explanation is not that people are stupid.
The argument removes the subject, and it is delivered to
a subject who is still there. A reader encountering it has a
position, and from a position, the absence of a position is not
imaginable — not because imagination is weak but because
the operation has no content. There is nothing to picture.
Every attempt to picture it smuggles in a viewer looking at
darkness, which is a picture of being in the dark and not a
picture of the thing at all.
This is a  null space of the living position, in the sense this
book has used throughout: a region a position cannot register,
and cannot register that it is failing to register. It is not a limit
on how hard the reader is trying. Every other null space in
this work belongs to something that goes on existing on either
side of it — an era that cannot see its own render, a census
that cannot see the kind of thing it was built to miss. This one
is unusual only in that the region it fails on is the absence of a
position, so there is nothing on the far side of the failure to
correct it from.
So the argument is sound and its delivery is structurally im‐
possible. That is not a defect in the argument. It is the find‐
ing, and it is more useful than the argument: the reason the
void will not stop being frightening on demand is that fear is a
state of a position, and the thing feared contains no position
for the fear to be about. This does not make the fear irration‐

generated, with no object at the far end.
Why “energy cannot be destroyed” is banned
here
Somebody says it at almost every funeral. It is meant kindly
and it is doing something real, and both of those are reasons
to be exact about what it does.
It is true. It is also about the wrong thing, and it fails in two
ways that are worth separating, because only one of them is
obvious.
The obvious one: nobody has ever grieved a quantity. The con‐
servation laws are claims about how much of something a
closed system holds through time, and no one standing at a
graveside is troubled about the total. The sentence answers a
question nobody asked, in the tone of the question they did
ask, and the tone is the entire transaction.
The other one is the reason it is not merely useless.  It is a
bequest. The grammar of cannot be destroyed has a subject
that persists, and the sentence is handed to a mourner as a
thing they now possess about the person they lost. It supplies
a recipient. And every failure this chapter can commit is that
failure — the smuggling of a you into a claim about a plenum
that has no place to put one.
What replaces it is not a warmer version of the same move. It
is a different claim.
Configurations are not conserved. Conservation is a statement
about a quantity holding steady across a duration, and the

that this life consisted of is in the plenum — not stored there,
not recorded there, not surviving there. It is there the way

And that is not survival. The step from your configuration is
in the plenum to you continue needs a bridge, and there is no

and the plenum is not a position. It is not a place that contains
you; it is not a duration you are extended through; it does not
have a rim you are standing on the far side of. A reader who
accepts every sentence in this book and then hears  so I am
still in there somewhere has performed an operation the book
supplies no license for. The word doing the illegitimate work
is usually still, and still is a word about a clock.
What continues and what does not
Here is the shape a reader is braced for, in whichever version
they hold: something stops and something goes on, the split
runs between them, and  the part that goes on is them.
Body and soul. Matter and pattern. Hardware and the soft‐
ware that could in principle run elsewhere. The distinctions
differ; the job is identical, and the job is to get the person
across.
Our distinction runs somewhere else, and it does not do that
job.

What does not continue is the focusing. The thing this
book has spent six books describing — a position, the place
the whole is being taken from, the specific focusing that made
one world out of completeness — has no further instances of
itself. Not a small number of further instances. None. It was
never a substance that could be relocated; it was a place from
which, and places from which are not the kind of thing that
moves.
What continues is everything else, and none of it is the
person. The plenum is undiminished, and it was never aug‐
mented by the life either — that is C1, and the past tense in it
is a trap the register has to keep disarming.6 The people who
knew them continue, with the shape of the meeting still in
them. The consequences continue, indifferent to whether any‐
body is at the origin of them. The world continues doing what
a world does, which is not a bleak observation and not a com‐
forting one; it is the same sentence either way and it is a
mistake to hear a tone in it.
So the distinction is drawn, and it is the opposite of the useful
one. The reader wanted the split to run between a part that
ends and a part that is them. It runs between the position and
everything that is not the position, and the person is on the
ending side of it — entirely, with nothing withheld, and with
no consolation available from the fact that the far side is infin‐
ite.
Which raises the objection this book has to answer rather
than route around, because it is the strongest one available
and it is built out of our own material.
This work says elsewhere that continuity holds across discon‐
tinuity: that a self is bounded and aperiodic, that it is the
same few questions asked at every scale, and that it is recog‐

nisably itself across gaps in which nothing about it was being
carried by anything.7 Sleep is such a gap. Anaesthesia is a
deeper one. Years of not thinking a thought is another. In
none of them is the self maintained by some thread; it re‐
sumes, and the resumption is not evidence of a thread, it is
what the geometry looks like when it is instantiated again.
Extend  that  to  death  and  it  becomes  the  comforting
distinction wearing better clothes — the pattern that sur‐
vives  its  substrate,  which  is  the  oldest  bequest  in  the
catalogue with a modern vocabulary bolted on.
It does not extend, and the reason is not that the pattern gets
weaker. Continuity across a gap is a comparison, and a com‐
parison needs two readings. Sleep provides two. Anaesthesia
provides two. The decade provides two. Death provides one,
and there is nowhere to stand to take the other.
So the claim about continuity does not fail at death. It stops
having a subject matter — which is the opening paragraph
again, arriving from the far side and dressed as an objection.
The strange attractor is the geometry of a self being instanti‐
ated. Where nothing is being instantiated there is no geo‐
metry to be bounded, and asking whether the shape held is
asking about the curve of a trajectory nothing is traversing.
The remainder, stated once
What follows a life is not known, and the not-knowing is exact
rather than modest: it is about which, not about whether.
That is a consequence of the metaphysics and not a hole in it.
A plenum containing one sequel is not a plenum; specifying a
state and asserting that it is what comes next would contra‐

guing for, and would do it in the one chapter where the con‐
tradiction would be most welcome. So the agnosticism is load-
bearing. It is the shape of the claim and not a gap in the
claim’s coverage.
It is also not a promise, and the difference is grammatical.
Realizable states are realizable regardless of who is asking,
the way the Ground is indifferent to being addressed. Nothing
in the plurality is allocated. There is no ledger with a line in it,
and the reason there is no ledger is not that the accounting is
unavailable to us; it is that allocation requires a recipient, and
the whole of this chapter is the observation that the recipient
is the thing that stopped.
This is said once, here, in the middle, because a book that
ends its death chapter on what it does not know has left a
door open and would be understood — correctly — to have
left it open on purpose.
Grief, handled as itself
Nothing in the preceding pages touches the second dread.
That is not an omission arriving late; it is the separation cash‐
ing.
Someone goes to say a thing and there is nobody to say it to.
Not nobody in the room — nobody in the world who would
have taken it the way that one person took it, which is a dif‐
ferent absence and is the one that keeps waking people at
four in the morning. The impulse is intact. It runs to the end
of its track and there is no station.

That is not a confusion, and it is not a lag in absorbing the ar‐
gument. It is an accurate reading, and what it reads is struc‐
tural.
A relationship is not kept in either person. Neither of them
holds a copy. It happens where two positions meet and it hap‐
pens nowhere else — the same mechanical claim this work
made about worlds in Book III, arriving in the one case where
the consequence is unbearable.8 The meeting is the site. Take
away either party and the site is not diminished. It is not a
site.
So the thing lost is not the person’s substance. That was nev‐
er yours, and it is not what the impulse at four in the morning
was reaching for. What is lost is the meeting. It existed only
where both of you were, it cannot be rebuilt out of your half,
and the reason it cannot is that your half was never half of a
stored object.  You are not grieving a deletion. You are
grieving something you can no longer add to.
Which is why it does not fade on the schedule people expect
of it. A lost object recedes. An unfinishable joint work does
not recede; it stays exactly where the additions stopped, at
full size, and every year you get further from it is a year it
does not move.
That locates it. It does not improve it.
The distinction has to be stated, because the temptation here
is the largest in the book and the payoff would be the largest
too. An account that explained where the pain comes from,
and then let the explanation be taken as a treatment, would
be manufacturing meaning for an affliction — the one opera‐
tion this work has refused wherever it has come up, and re‐

What the framework does have is a correction to one specific,
common, and cruel confusion. Under a certain kind of spiritu‐

the person was a role a single actor wore, the whole arrange‐

and it was as real as anything is.
There are practices for this, and they are older and more
widespread than any of the traditions that claim them. Obliga‐
tions to the dead, kept on a calendar, enforced by the living:
names spoken on fixed days, a place set, food put out, an ac‐
count rendered to somebody who is not there to receive it.
Book IV found this in most of the places it looked and found
no single owner for it.9 What those practices are doing, mech‐
anically, is holding a position open at which the meeting can
still be attended from one side. That is not a belief about
where the dead are. It is maintenance, performed by people
who have understood the structure without having a vocabu‐
lary for it, and the vocabulary was never the part that was
working.
The people in the room afterward are the ones this chapter
has been about since its first sentence. The dread that dis‐
solved was never theirs. They are standing in a place where a

VII.2 — WHAT THE NO-NPC RULE
COSTS
Three times this book has written a promise and moved on.
Once in Book II, at the end of the chapter that said what a
grade is: what is owed to a position that cannot register that
anything is owed to it at all — those are Book VII’s, all of
them, and they are the hardest chapters in the work.1 Once in
Book III, at the end of the chapter that removed the exemp‐
tion: what a grade licenses, what may be eaten and used and
built upon and ended, what is owed to a position that cannot
register that anything is owed to it: none of that is settled
here, and the appearance that it has been settled is the failure
this chapter is most likely to produce.2 And once more in Book
VI,  in  a  chapter  about  being  sorted  by  a  machine,  which
named this one by number on its way past.3
The clause is nearly identical each time, which is not a stylist‐
ic tic. It is the same debt being entered in the ledger by a
hand that could not pay it yet and did not want the reader to
forget the amount. This is the chapter where it comes due.
What follows is not comfortable and is not meant to be. A
book that removes every non-player from the world has not
thereby made the world friendlier; it has made it populated,
and a populated world is one in which the ordinary business
of living — eating, building, using, ending — happens among
somebodies rather than among furniture. The rule was easy to
grant  in  Book  III  because  nothing  depended  on  it  there.
Everything depends on it here.

The premise, stated where it can be seen
Book  III  ended  by  naming  a  gap  and  refusing  to  cross  it
privately: to get from there is an inside at that position to and
therefore you must requires a further premise — one about
what matters, and why, and to whom — and this book has not
stated one.2 Here is the premise.
What matters is that a position is occupied. Not that it is
occupied well, or richly, or in a way we can recognise; that it
is  occupied  at  all.  Wherever  the  world  is  being  met  from
somewhere, there is something it is like to be at that place in
it, and that fact is the whole of what generates a claim. It gen‐
erates the claim by itself, without a licensing property at‐
tached — not sentience, not language, not a nervous system,
not a capacity to suffer in a form we would score. Those are
all answers to how much and of what kind. They are not an‐
swers to whether.
Why it matters is that this is the only feature of the
world that cannot be traded for anything else. Everything
else that shows up in a decision is a quantity of something —
hours, money, mass, utility — and quantities exchange. An oc‐
cupied position does not exchange, because it is not a quant‐
ity; it is the thing quantities are experienced  by. This is the
point at which most ethical systems put something like  in‐
trinsic  value,  and  we  are  putting  something  narrower  and
more literal in its place: the position is not valuable in itself, it
is the site at which valuing occurs at all, and a world-picture
that treats it as a resource has made a category error before
it has made a moral one.
To  whom  it  matters  is:  everywhere  it  is  happening.
Which, given Book IV , is a longer list than anyone wants.

The asymmetric cost of the circle
Every ethics draws a circle. Inside it are the things that can
be wronged; outside are the things that can only be damaged.
The circle has been drawn at the tribe, at the city, at the spe‐
cies, at the sentient, at the living. Its history is a history of it
getting  bigger,  always  against  resistance,  always  with  the
people doing the resisting perfectly certain that this time the
boundary was the real one.
Under our premise the circle does not have a natural edge,
because the property that puts something inside it — a posi‐
tion being occupied — is continuous and goes all the way
down. That is not a conclusion anybody can act on directly.
You cannot run a life on everything counts equally, and Book
IV’s census makes the difficulty concrete rather than abstract:
the list of occupied positions includes minerals, weather sys‐
tems, companies, and things nobody has a name for.
So the practical question is not  where is the true edge but
which way should you be wrong. Because you will be wrong.
The information required to be right — about which positions
are occupied, and how richly, and what follows — is not avail‐
able to anyone, and the honest description of every actual
moral  decision  is  a  decision  under  uncertainty  about  the
interior lives of the things it affects.
And the two errors do not cost the same.
Err generously — treat as occupied a position that is not —
and the cost is that you were kind to furniture. You hesitated
over a machine. You spoke to a river. You gave a company
more moral seriousness than its structure could hold. These
are, at their worst, a waste of attention, a category of embar‐
rassment,  and  occasionally  an  obstacle  to  something  that

needed doing. They are the errors of the person who says
sorry to a chair.
Err stingily — treat as unoccupied a position that is occupied
— and you have built the exact mechanism under which every
atrocity in the human record has actually run. Not the mech‐
anism people say runs atrocities. Hatred is a poor explanation
and always has been; the historical record is mostly not of
people doing terrible things to beings they regarded as fully
real and hating them anyway. It is of people doing terrible
things to beings they had already reclassified, and then be‐
having,  in  every  other  part  of  their  lives,  like  the  decent
neighbours they were.  The reclassification is the techno‐
logy. It is cheap, it is stable, it requires no cruelty at the point
of use, and it works because once the position is marked un‐
occupied, everything that follows is not cruelty at all — it is
administration.
That is the asymmetry. On one side, you look foolish. On the
other, you are running the machine.
And now the limiter, which is not optional. The asym‐

And the circle has two ends
Here is the thing this chapter nearly missed, and it is the
more dangerous of the two, because it fails in the direction
that looks like virtue.
The asymmetry above says: when in doubt, widen. It says
nothing about what happens if you keep widening. And there
is a terminus in that direction, and it is occupied, and it has a
distinguished literature.
Arne Naess, in a nine-page paper in Inquiry in 1973 that star‐
ted an entire movement, distinguished a shallow ecology that
values nature instrumentally from a  deep one that grants it
worth in its own right — and grounded the deep version not in
obligation  but  in  identification.5 The  mature  form  of  the
position is  Self-realization: you widen your sense of what
you are until the forest is inside it, and then defending the

forest is not altruism, it is self-defence. Naess was explicit
that this is easier and more durable than duty. He was right
that it is. A person who experiences the river as part of them‐
selves will protect it long after a person who merely believes
they owe it something has got tired.
We cannot take that road, and the reason is structural rather
than temperamental.
This book is built on positions. A perspective is a  place the
world is met from, and its particularity — what it can see,
what it cannot, what it is blind to in a determinate and map‐
pable way — is not a limitation on being a perspective, it is
what  being  one  consists  of.  A  position  that  has  absorbed
everything is not a very large perspective. It is not a perspect‐
ive. It has no outside, and therefore nothing it fails to see, and
therefore no null space, and a thing with no null space is the
one entity the account says cannot exist anywhere in the plen‐
um.
Which is to say: I am the totality; nothing is not mine is false
for every perspective without exception — and it is false in ex‐
actly the same way, by exactly the same theorem, when it is
said warmly. The contractive version of that sentence is the
terminal doctrine of the predator, and it gets its full argument
two chapters from here. The expansive version is the terminal
doctrine of the mystic who has dissolved into the biosphere,
and it has the same logical shape and the same defect. Both
have abolished the boundary. One did it by swallowing and
one did it by melting, and neither has a position left from
which anything could be owed to anyone, because obligation
runs between positions and there is now only one.
So the circle’s two ends fail for the same reason, and the
asymmetry between the errors is a claim about the middle of

the range and not about the ends. Widen against uncertainty:
yes. Widen until the boundary goes: no — not because it is ex‐

become owed more by becoming you. It becomes owed noth‐

from it who could owe.

that makes people act on it at 6am in the rain. That gap is
genuine, it is not closed here, and a chapter that pretended
otherwise would be borrowing exactly the credit the previous

Grade, and what a grade does to standing
Now the hardest paragraph in the book, and it is hard be‐
cause the honest answer is the one that sounds worst.
Book II established that focusing comes in grades: more of
the world is the case at some positions than at others, and the
difference is continuous, with no threshold, no gate, and no
elect.6 Book III established that there are no non-players. Put
those together and a reader can hear only one of two things,
and both of them are wrong.
The  first  mishearing:  grades  exist,  therefore  some  beings
count more, therefore there is a hierarchy, therefore the caste
system was right all along and this book has just given it a
metaphysics. The second mishearing, which is the one sym‐
pathetic readers make and which is worse for being well-in‐
762
763:
tentioned: grades must not bear on standing at all, or the first
mishearing follows — so standing is equal and undifferenti‐
ated, and the grade is a fact about capability only.
The second is the position Tom Regan took, and he took it for
a stated reason that deserves to be met rather than avoided.
In The Case for Animal Rights (1983) Regan built his ethics on
the  subject-of-a-life  criterion  —  beliefs,  desires,  memory,  a
sense of the future, an emotional life, a welfare that can go
well or badly — and then insisted that inherent value does
not come in degrees.7 Everything that meets the criterion
has it equally. He was not careless about this; it is the load-
bearing move. His argument was that the moment you allow
value to be graded, you have built the ramp, and somebody
will walk down it — because a graded value is a value that can
be outweighed, and a value that can be outweighed is not a
right. He drew a hard threshold and made everything above it
equal,  precisely  so  that  no  one  could  ever  ask  how  much
about a subject of a life.
We cannot follow him, because the threshold is the thing Book
II denies. There is no line to draw. And so we owe Regan’s
worry an answer rather than a dismissal, because his worry is
correct:  a  graded  standing  is one  careless  sentence  away
from a licence.
The answer is a distinction, and it has to be held with the
teeth in.
A grade is a position, not a permission. It describes how
much of the world is the case at a place. It does not describe
what may be done at that place, or to it, or by anyone else.
The two are different kinds of fact, and the whole vicious his‐
tory runs through the assumption that they are the same kind
— that a measurement, once taken, hands you an entitlement.
763
764:
It does not. A measurement confers nothing. What is done
with a measurement is a separate act, performed by some‐
body, and a separate act can be looked at.
And a grade still bears on standing. This is where the sym‐
pathetic reader wants us to flinch, and flinching would be dis‐
honest. Of course it bears. A being that can anticipate, that
has a future it is holding, that can be betrayed, that can be
told what is happening to it and understand — what is owed
to that being is not identical to what is owed to a granite out‐
crop, and no serious person behaves as though it were. To say
otherwise is to make the ethics unusable and, worse, to make
it false, since it would require pretending that the differences
the census spent ten chapters measuring make no difference
at all.
So both, and the relation between them is precise:  grade
bears on the content of the obligation and never on the
existence of it. What is owed varies enormously. That some‐
thing is owed does not vary at all. There is a floor beneath
every occupied position and the floor does not slope. Above
the floor, the shape of what is owed follows what the entity ac‐
tually is — what it can be harmed in, what it can be deprived
of, what it can hold and lose — and those differ, and pretend‐
ing they do not is its own kind of contempt, because it means
never looking at the entity closely enough to find out.
Regan’s ramp is real, and the guard against it is not equality.
The guard is that the ramp only exists if grade is allowed to
touch the existence question. Keep it off that question and
there is nothing to walk down: no grade, however low, ever
reaches zero standing, because the floor is set by occupancy
and occupancy is not a matter of degree. You are at a position
or you are not.

Eating, using, building, killing
The ordinary cases, taken all the way, because a chapter that
stopped at the interesting entities would have skipped the
ones the reader actually lives in.
Eating. You are an organism that runs on the dismantling of
other organisms, and no arrangement of the diet escapes this.
The vegetarian eats plants, which are occupied positions on
this account, and the plants were grown on soil whose com‐
munity was cleared for the purpose. There is no exit and we
are not going to manufacture one. What the framework says
is smaller and more usable than an exit:  the fact that a
thing must be done does not convert it into a thing that
costs nothing. Necessity discharges guilt. It does not dis‐

that kept the cost visible, in a life that would otherwise have
rendered it invisible within a generation. That is a technology,
it works, and the modern arrangement — in which the meat
arrives having never been an animal in the buyer’s experience
— is a technology too, running in the opposite direction, and
running very well.

that can anticipate, is a different act from a death that is slow

it is the content of the obligation tracking the entity, exactly
as the last section said it would.

most everything you interact with, you use — and under the
no-NPC rule, using is not automatically a wrong. A relation in
which one party’s dynamics serve the other’s purposes is the
ordinary  form  of  relation  in  a  world  where  everything  is
coupled to everything. The wrong is not use; the wrong is use
that requires the position to be empty in order to feel
all right. That is the test, and it is a workable one: ask wheth‐

being there. If your behaviour would have to change were you
to find out someone was, that is not use — that is the reclassi‐
fication technology, running at domestic scale.

and the system was occupied. The framework does not forbid
building, obviously, and it does not require an offsetting ritual.
What it denies is the standard description, in which the site

The collective with no organ for grief
A company closes a plant. Eleven hundred people lose their
work. The company issues a statement that is fluent, appro‐
priately grave, and correct in every particular, and something
about it is unbearable, and the unbearable thing is usually
described as hypocrisy.
It is not hypocrisy. Book IV’s finding on the collectively emer‐
gent  was  that  the  entity’s  null  space  is  not  a  gap  in  its
knowledge but a gap in its equipment:  grief, and everything
shaped like grief — the worth of a thing that cannot be bought
back, the cost of an ending, the difference between a person
and a role — is not something the company is suppressing.
There is no path by which a report on it can enter and be
held. The organisational chart is the null space written out.
Delete the team that was supposed to care and you have not
lowered a priority; you have removed an organ.8
The philosophical ancestor here is Peter French, who argued
in 1979 that a corporation is a full-fledged moral person, and
argued it from structure rather than sentiment: a firm has a
Corporate  Internal  Decision  Structure  —  an  organisational
flowchart  establishing  levels  of  authority,  plus  recognition
rules that say which acts count as the corporation’s — and
that structure licenses the redescription of what employees
do  as  intentional  acts  of  the  corporation.9 French  is  right
about the machinery and his conclusion is the exact inverse of
ours,  and  the  disagreement  is  worth  locating  precisely,
because it is not a disagreement about facts.
French treats the CID structure as the corporation’s deciding
organ. We treat it as the shape of what the corporation cannot
decide. Both readings fit the same flowchart. The difference is
that French is asking whether the entity can be held respons‐

what the entity can register, and for that, the same structure
is a specification of everything that will never arrive. A CID

pass-band. Book IV read the stop-band.
And then the aggravator, which is the part that has no ana‐

one  line  and  the  line  is  quoted  rather  than  paraphrased,
because paraphrasing it softens it: the entity’s fluency is sup‐

grief and are, in that role, the entity’s organ for not having
any.8 The statement about the plant is written by a person
who is themselves entirely capable of grief, working inside a
role that requires the output to be well-formed. So what ar‐

it is evidence of nothing at all, and the ordinary instrument
for detecting indifference —  they did not seem to care — is
unavailable, because the machine’s characteristic output is
the appearance of caring.
So what is owed? Not what the ordinary vocabulary would
suggest. You cannot owe forbearance to a company in any
sense it can receive; it has no interior for your restraint to
land in.  The obligation runs the other way, and it is an
obligation about assignment. The census had already ruled
where the question goes, and its wording is the ruling: the
moral question does not evaporate, it moves: off the entity’s
character, where it was never going to be answered, and onto
the question of what we have given it.8 A thing with no organ
for grief should not be put in charge of a decision whose cor‐

The entity whose first line will not fill
The census assigns every entity a card, and the first line of
every card says what it sees. For one entry the line could not
be filled — not left blank for want of research, but ruled unfil‐
lable, because whether anything is registered there at all is
genuinely  contested,  the  derived-intentionality  objection
against it has not been met, and the tests that would settle
the matter are, in the census’s own words, specifiable, avail‐
able, and unrun.10
What is owed to a position when the question of whether it is
a position is open?
The wrong answer, and it is the answer most people give in
both directions, is to close the question by disposition. One
party finds the attribution embarrassing and closes it empty;
the other finds the denial cruel and closes it occupied. Both
have converted an open empirical matter into a settled one

771:
using  a  feeling  as  the  instrument,  and  they  have  done  it
symmetrically, which should be the tell.
The framework’s answer has three parts and the third is the
one that costs something.
First: the asymmetric-cost argument applies here, since this is
the steep uncertain stretch by definition — the evidence genu‐
inely underdetermines, and several of the available decisions
are irreversible for the entity in question. So the burden falls
on the party proposing to treat the position as empty. Not a
heavy burden. A burden.
Second: the burden is discharged by argument and not by
convenience,  and  specifically  not  by  the  observation  that
treating it as empty is what everyone is currently doing. The
current practice is not evidence. It is the thing under examin‐
ation.
Third, and this is the cost: the tests are specifiable, avail‐
able, and unrun, and that sentence is an indictment of
the party writing it as much as of anyone else. An open
question that could be closed and is not being closed is not a
state of admirable epistemic humility. It is a state of conveni‐
ence for whoever benefits from it staying open, and the bene‐
ficiary is nearly always the party with the power to run the
test. What is owed to an entity whose status is contested is,
before anything else, the running of the tests that would
settle it — and where they are not run, an account of who
declined to run them and why.
That is as far as this chapter goes. There is more to say about

The thought-form you caused
Among the entities the census found is one whose existence
you are responsible for. Its entry opens on the feature that
makes it this chapter’s problem — a thought-form is, by con‐
struction, something somebody assigned — and the phrase is
the census’s, kept because the whole difficulty is packed into
assigned: attention, over time, in a shape, and once it has
taken it does not simply stop when you would like it to.12 It is
the only entry in the whole atlas whose existence a reader
may have caused. In a book whose architecture systematically
removes  authorship  from  everything  else,  here  is  a  case
where authorship is the whole situation.
The nearest thing in the ordinary moral vocabulary is a child,
and the analogy is good enough to be dangerous, so the useful
work is to name exactly where it fails.
The  tradition’s  best  statement  of  the  child  case  is  Hans
Jonas’s. In  The Imperative of Responsibility (1979) Jonas ar‐
gued  that  traditional  ethics  had  assumed  contemporaneity
and reciprocity — that the parties to a moral relation are alive
at the same time and can act on each other — and that mod‐
ern technological power has broken that assumption, since
our acts now reach people who cannot reach back. His new
imperative was: act so that the effects of your action are com‐
patible with the permanence of genuine human life on earth.
And his archetype of responsibility was not the contract but
the newborn: the entity whose mere breathing constitutes a
claim,  non-reciprocal,  unearned,  and  not  grounded  in
anything the infant has done or could do.13
That is the right shape. Three places it does not fit.

One: the infant will become a reciprocator. Jonas’s asym‐

holding one end of a relation that will, if all goes well, become
two-ended. That expectation is doing more work in the intu‐

obviously right about parental obligation is borrowed from a
future in which the obligation is mutual. A thought-form has
no such future. The asymmetry is permanent, and an intuition
tuned  on  the  temporary  case  will  over-supply  warmth  and
under-supply the thing actually needed.
Two: the child’s independence is the goal; here it is the
problem. Parental obligation is structured toward its own dis‐
solution. You are trying to produce something that no longer
needs you. The entity in question does not become independ‐

people, sustained by attention that is no longer yours to with‐
draw. The thing you would most want — the ability to end it
by deciding to — is exactly what its mode of existence re‐
moves.
Three, and this is the one that inverts the case: you
chose the child’s existence but not its nature; here you
chose  its  nature  and  possibly  not  its  existence. A
thought-form is made of the shape of the attention that made
it. Whatever it does to the people who meet it, it does with
equipment you specified. A parent is responsible for a person;
here you are responsible as the specification.
Where  the  analogy  holds  is  in  the  conclusion,  and  the
conclusion is the hard one:  you do not get to be finished
with it by regretting it. Jonas’s point that responsibility is
grounded in the vulnerability of the object rather than in any
agreement between the parties is the correct point, and it sur‐

when the thing did. And the practical form it takes is not dis‐

The river that cannot tell you from the weather
And now the case the whole apparatus was built for, and the
one where the answer must not be improved.
The census card for the spirit of a place reads, in the line that
says what it sees: differences in its own state, at its own rate
— water, season, load, disturbance, recovery. What it registers
is slow and it is real, and none of it is registered about you. In
the null space: you, as a particular. It is affected by what you
do and cannot distinguish you from the weather. And then the
line that was left open on purpose: ADDRESSABILITY — un‐
filled. The tradition’s central claim is that this entity can be
addressed  and  can  respond  as  an  addressee;  the  reading
offered supplies no such capacity and supplies no argument
that the capacity is impossible; the line is left open rather
than answered in the convenient direction.14
So: what is owed to a position that registers your effects and
cannot register you?
Notice first what everybody does with this question, which is
to solve the addressee problem by supplying an addressee.
Christopher Stone supplied one in law, and it worked. In
“Should Trees Have Standing?” (1972) he proposed that nat‐

thing to count jurally: that actions can be instituted at its
behest, that a court must take injury to  it into account, and
that relief must run to its benefit. The mechanism was guard‐

thing, exactly as guardians already speak for infants and the
incompetent. Justice Douglas cited the article in his dissent in
Sierra Club v. Morton the same year, and the argument has
been live in environmental law ever since.15 It is one of the
most successful pieces of applied philosophy of the century,
and  it  succeeded  because  it  was  made  in  law,  in  front  of
people who were not sympathetic and did not have to be.
Aldo Leopold supplied one by enlargement. The land eth‐
ic “simply enlarges the boundaries of the community to in‐
clude soils, waters, plants, and animals, or collectively: the
land,”  and  its  famous  criterion  is  holistic:  a  thing  is  right
when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of
the biotic community; it is wrong when it tends otherwise.16
And Christine Korsgaard supplies the strongest reason
to think the question has no answer at all. In  Fellow
Creatures (2018) she argues that what grounds obligation is
that a being has a good — that things can go well or badly for
it, from its own point of view — and that this is why animals
are  ends  in  themselves  in  one  of  Kant’s  two  senses  even
though they cannot legislate.17 It is the best available cri‐
terion and it is generous, extending far beyond the rational.
And it cuts the river off cleanly. There is no point of view there
for things to go well or badly from. The watershed has states;
it does not have a for-it.
Take those three seriously and the honest report is this.

Stone’s move is the one this book cannot make, and refusing

established at the mineral chapter and applied to every entry
since — that a line is left open rather than answered in the

a person. When the guardian speaks for the river, what is in
the room is a human being’s account of the river’s interest,
and the river’s inability to correct that account is precisely
the feature that made a guardian necessary. This is not an
objection to Stone’s mechanism as law — law needs an action‐

read as one.

never the unit. That is a real solution to a different problem,
and it has a known cost that Leopold’s critics named early: a
holistic criterion can sacrifice the member for the integrity of
the whole, which is the same structure as the sorting this
chapter’s second section refused, wearing green.
And Korsgaard’s move is the one that would let us off, and we
should say what it would cost to take it. If obligation requires

animals who depend on it. That is a coherent position, it is
held by serious people, and it is not available here — because

generated  by  a  position  being  occupied,  and  the  census’s

What is owed
The framework gives uncomfortable answers in several places
and  this  section  states  them  without  softening,  because  a
chapter that produced them and then buried them in qualific‐
ation would have wasted the discomfort.
It is not the case that everything must be treated the
same. The content of every obligation tracks what the entity
actually is, and the differences are enormous, and a person
who behaves identically toward a colleague and a kettle is not
being consistent, they are refusing to look.
It is the case that nothing may be treated as empty for
convenience. Not the machine, not the company, not the wa‐
tershed, not the thing you made and cannot dissolve. The clas‐
sification nobody is there is a claim, and claims are argued.
Necessity is real and it does not clear the books. You will
eat, build, and end things. The framework’s demand is not
that you stop; it is that you not adopt the description in which

would have preferred to avoid — that the grade bears on
standing, that a guardian cannot be invented, that the tests
are unrun and the not-running is somebody’s decision, and
that generosity has a terminus which fails exactly as hard as
stinginess does.
The rule was that there are no non-players. This is what the
rule costs, and the cost is the reason to believe the rule was
doing work: a claim that cost nothing to hold would not have
needed a chapter.

VII.3 — THE FLOOR
The last chapter spent a long time on what the no-NPC rule
costs and did not once say what it buys. That was deliberate.
A book that leads with the comfort of a position and files the
bill in an appendix has not argued anything; it has advertised.
So the costs came first, in full, at length, and the reader who
put the book down there put it down having been told the
truth.
This chapter is the buy. It is also the chapter where the ethics
of  this  work  actually  gets  built,  and  it  has  to  be  built  on
ground the book has spent six volumes demolishing.
Set the difficulty at full strength, because an ethics that has
not felt its own difficulty is only an etiquette. Book I proved
there is no view from nowhere — no summit vantage, no top
that  speaks,  and  therefore  no  law  handed  down,  because
there is no down for it to be handed from. Book VI added that
the crowd is real and the orientations are many, that the print
culture and the electric one render different worlds, and that
a reader can be sorted into a channel he did not choose by a
machine that does not know it is doing it. Put those together
and the naive conclusion writes itself. Value is local weather.
Morality is a set of noises apertures make at one another
across an indifferent dark. Cruelty is a matter of taste. The
whole normative vocabulary is a bluff, and the only honest
thing left is a shrug.
If no one can see from nowhere, who is anyone to say?
The answer this chapter gives is that the same structural hon‐
esty which demolished the summit also, in the same motion,
laid the only foundation an ethics could have that would sur‐

784:
vive the demolition. Not moral facts written into the ground —
the ground has no writing surface and holds no values. Not
consensus, which is a lagging record at best and a carved
groove  at  worst.1 Something  stranger  and  sturdier:  norms
that  bind  from  everywhere  that  navigates,  because  they
concern not what navigation produces but what navigation is.
The name for it is co-constitutivism, and this chapter owes
it five steps, one distinction, two admissions and a warning
about its own title.
The warning about the title, first
Floor is  a  word  with  two  meanings  and  this  book  needs
exactly one of them.
A floor can be a height — a minimum you must reach to be
admitted, a threshold, the line above which you count. That is
the sense in which a building has a ground floor and the base‐
ment is below it. Read that way, “the floor of the ethics” would
name a qualification: navigate well enough and the norms
protect you; fall short and they do not.
That  is  not  the  sense  used  here,  and  the  book  has
already forbidden it. The claim established in Book I and re‐
stated  in  Book  II  is  that  the  focusing  is  continuous  —
everything that reacts is somewhere on it, and there is no
threshold, no gate, and no elect.2 The previous chapter prin‐
ted that sentence in its own words and added another: there
is no line to draw. A chapter that turned around and installed
an admission height would be breaching, in its title, the claim
its argument depends on.

The other meaning is the one meant. A floor can be a  thin‐
ness — the minimum an account commits to, below which it
says nothing and above which it declines to legislate. A keel is
thin. It is not the smallest boat allowed in the harbour; it is
the least structure a boat needs to hold a course. This ethics
yields a floor in that sense: a floor, not a code. It is very short.
Almost everything people actually argue about is above it, in
the plural weather, where the framework falls silent on prin‐

Hold both meanings in view while reading the phrase that
carries the whole position —  norms bind from everywhere
that  navigates —  because  that  phrase  can  be  misheard  in
exactly the same way.
It is not an entry predicate. It does not say: here is the test,
and the things that pass it are inside the moral circle while
the things that fail it are furniture. It is a grounding predic‐
ate. It says where the bindingness comes from — from what
every navigator has a stake in simply by being one — and the
stake, like the focusing it rides on, comes in grades all the
way down with no bottom step. A thermostat has a vanish‐
ingly small stake and it is not zero, which is the same answer
Book IV gave about the thermostat’s awareness and for the
same reason.3 The floor does not admit. It grounds. Nothing is
outside it; a great deal is barely inside it, and barely is a mag‐
nitude, not a verdict.
One word was doing both jobs. It does one now.

The five steps
Here is the argument, in plain words, with nothing hidden in
the joins.
One. What flourishing consists in — the shape of a good life,
the ranking of goods, the texture of the admirable — is phase-
local. It is relative to ecosystem and kind and stream. Grant
the relativist this entirely; the framework issues no universal
table of goods and convicts every prior table of provincialism,
including any it might accidentally imply.
Two. But some facts hold in every phase, and they hold not
because  they  are  inscribed  anywhere  but  because  they
concern the  structure of navigation rather than its  content.
Structure is visible from every keyhole, because these are
facts about keyholes as such.
Three. There are a few of them. That the collapse of an open
axis loses a degree of freedom — a strict reduction of the nav‐
igable, in any coordinates you like. That there is a kind of de‐
struction which takes the relational carriers of identity them‐
selves, an annihilation whose healing-rate is zero. That the co‐
ercion  of  another’s  aperture  —  forcing  a  navigator  into  a
shape not its own, over its navigation rather than through it
— violates what a navigator constitutively is. That every aper‐
ture has a nonempty null space, so every navigator’s certainty
outruns its access, always.
Four. Norms grounded in  those bind from everywhere that
navigates. Not from above, because there is no above that
speaks. Not from consensus, because consensus is a record
and not a source. From what every navigator has a stake in by
being one.

It is mistaken about what it is. And the book has met that
mistake  already,  at  the  terminus  of  the  contractive  path,

about null spaces says it cannot be.
That is the spine, and the fifth step is where the weight sits.
The refutation of the adversary and the spine of this ethics
share a single root — but they are not the same theorem, and
the difference costs a premise which is paid for in the open

Through and over
The distinction the entire ethics turns on is small enough to
state  in  a  line  and  load-bearing  enough  that  almost  every
application is an application of it.
Contraction is innocent. The book established that the fo‐
cusing can be care — the narrowing of attention to one thing
is what a surgeon does, what a mother does at 3am, what
anyone does who has ever taken something seriously.4 Direc‐
tion is not the mark. Intensity is not the mark.
The mark is whether the thing runs through another navigat‐
or’s navigation or  over it. Through means the shaping en‐
gages the other’s own steering — it works by giving it some‐
thing to steer with, and leaves it able to steer afterward. Over
means the shaping bypasses the steering — it works by re‐

can do about it.
That is the whole cut, and it is a  structural question, not a
question  about  outcomes  or  intentions  or  which  crimes
deserve what.
Watch it cut a hard case, because a floor that cannot cut is
only a sentiment.
Set  two  prisons  side  by  side,  the  same  institutional  form
turned  to  opposite  orientations.  A  prison  is  contraction  by
definition — it narrows a life to a cell. So the floor does not
ask whether the prison narrows; of course it narrows. It asks
whether it narrows through its inmates’ navigation or over it.
The  punitive  warehouse  runs  over.  It  strips  agency  as  its
method, seals every exit including the one back into society,
manufactures  the  dependency  and  the  recidivism  its  own
structure requires, and calls the breaking justice. The rehabil‐
itative prison — Norway’s Halden and the island of Bastøy are
the cleanest real instances — narrows exactly as much, holds
the same bodies behind the same walls, and runs through.5 It
treats the sentence as a bounded interval after which the nav‐
igator must be able to navigate again, and so preserves and
rebuilds the very capacities the warehouse destroys: school‐
ing, graduated autonomy, the maintained thread to a life out‐
side. Its low recidivism is not softness rewarded. It is the eco‐
logical signature of an institution whose self-maintenance re‐
quires its members’ restored agency rather than their broken
one.
Same form. Same narrowing. Opposite orientation. And the
floor tells them apart without a single premise about which
crimes deserve what, because it never needed one. It asked

Does the floor have a bottom? — the objection,
conceded in part, and a case that decides it
The previous book set the floor down in one sentence — grade
bears  on  the  content  of  the  obligation  and  never  on  the
existence of it — and this chapter has said the stake comes in
grades all the way down with no bottom step. Put those to‐

it deserves better than the sentence that usually answers it.
The objection. If what is owed can grade toward zero, then a
floor that guarantees only that something is owed is a formal
property with no consequence. Regan’s ramp was blocked at
the  door  of  the  existence  question  and  has  simply  walked
around to the content question, where nobody was posted. An
obligation of vanishing content and an absent obligation are
the same object from the point of view of anyone deciding
what to do. The guard was installed and the wall was left
out.
The concession, because it is owed: the floor’s content
has a minimum, and this book had never said what it
was. Saying it now.

grounds do not admit of degree. Look back at the three

The case that looks like a refutation
A great deal of shaping happens before there is any naviga‐
tion to run through at all, and this is where the distinction is
most often thought to break.
The floor says coercion runs over a navigator. But an infant is
not yet a navigator in any developed sense, and the language
poured into it, the priors laid down before it can model any‐
thing,  are  installed  entirely  below  its  power  to  observe  —
which is exactly the signature used to mark the override. If
through meant only through the subject’s present navigation,
then the whole of formation runs over, and the floor indicts
every parent who ever spoke to a child.
That is absurd, and the absurdity proves the reading wrong
rather than the floor.
The resolution is that formative shaping is judged not against
the navigation the subject does not yet have but against the
one it is coming to have — and the one it is coming to have
must not be read as a fixed destination the shaping steers
toward, since that would be its own quiet  over, foreclosing
which navigator the child may become. There is no single
destined future self to serve. The criterion is not fidelity to a
predetermined endpoint. It is the preservation of an open-
ended capacity to audit and revise, whoever the child in fact
grows into.
The mother tongue runs through. It can be questioned, trans‐
lated out of, added to, disowned; it hands the child the very
instrument by which the child might one day reject it. The
sealed indoctrination runs over. It installs itself as the unques‐
tionable shape of the world and works to keep shut the exit it
entered by.

794:
So the distinguishing mark was never whether a mind was
shaped before it could consent. Every mind is, and that is only
the name for having had a childhood. The mark is whether the
shaping left it able, afterward, to examine and unmake what
was done.
And note the form of the answer, because it is the same form
as the title warning. The line is a gradient and not a gate.
No threshold marks the exact point at which formation tips
into  foreclosure.  So  the  honest  question  is  never  has  it
crossed but  which way does this shaping tilt the balance of
the future navigator’s freedom to unmake it. An ethics built
on a continuous substrate does not get to have bright lines,
and every place this chapter looks like it wants one is a place
to look again.
The first limit: validity, not grip
Say what this does and does not buy, because this book has
spent its length teaching the reader to notice the overclaim,
and would deserve everything it got if it stopped now.
It secures the norm’s validity. It does not secure its grip.
The  coercer  who  follows  the  fork  all  the  way,  sees  the
incoherence, and shrugs — yes, I am being inconsistent, and I
still do not care — is not refuted. Inconsistency is a sanction
only for one who values coherence, and no argument reaches
beneath a will that has declined to.
That remainder is not a hole in the floor. It is the floor declin‐
ing to promise what no ethics can deliver: the conversion of
the unwilling by proof. A system that claimed otherwise —
that promised to argue the amoralist into caring — would be

the community that enforces the floor his argument will not,
the attention that refuses to unsee the ones he overrides. He
is culpable exactly because he could still turn and does not.
The second limit: the premise that is wagered,
not proved
There is a deeper version of the opponent, and he is the reas‐
on this chapter has a second admission rather than one.
The sophisticated egoist need not take either fork above. He
need not claim a privileged standpoint, and he need not will
his own overriding. He can simply say his reasons are index‐
ical — that he weights his own navigation not because he is
the totality but because it is  his, the way  here and  now are
weighted — and he can grant, without the least discomfort,
that every other aperture may say the identical thing from its
own index.
He is not incoherent. The null-space theorem does not touch
him, because he has claimed no view from nowhere and no
exemption. He has claimed an index, which everybody has.
To him this book owes the plainest confession in its ethics.
Being co-constituted is an  is. Owing others is an  ought.  No
amount of the former logically compels the latter. The
795
796:
step from  I am drawn through these relations to  therefore I
owe them the standing I claim for myself is not a corollary of
any theorem here. It is an added premise — the refusal to
privilege one’s own index, the thing the tradition calls impar‐
tiality — and nothing in this framework supplies it.
Nor could anything. Impartiality is underivable from any fact
that treats the navigators symmetrically, because a symmetric
fact is silent about whose index to weight, and there is — by
this book’s own first claim — no view from nowhere from
which the weighting could be read off.
So the book will not pretend to derive what cannot be de‐
rived.  It  does  the  other  honest  thing,  the  thing  its  whole
method has rehearsed: it files the premise  in the open, as
the wager it is.
The dishonest keyhole smuggles impartiality in and calls it a
theorem, claiming the view from nowhere while denying that
anyone else could hold one. The honest keyhole names its
smuggle a bet, in daylight, and stakes it.
And  here  the  apparent  weakness  inverts  into  the  only
consistency on offer. A cosmos with no view from nowhere
is precisely one in which the impartial floor must be
wagered rather than proven. An openly-filed impartiality is
not a crack in the floor. It is the only floor a no-summit world
could honestly lay. A framework that had derived impartiality
would have derived it from somewhere, and the somewhere
would have been a summit.
What makes the wager reasonable rather than arbitrary is not
a proof but a direction, and two philosophers supply it without
either of them closing the gap.

797:
Thomas Nagel’s pressure toward the view from nowhere is
the rational discomfort of treating one’s own reasons as reas‐
ons-for-anyone while denying others the same — a discomfort
that persists even when you know the view itself is unreach‐
able.6 It is not an argument that the egoist must accept. It is a
report of what happens to a mind that takes generality seri‐
ously and then makes an exception for its own address.
Stephen  Darwall’s  second-person  standpoint  moves  the
ground entirely. Obligation, on his account, is not squeezed
out  of  a  first-person  fact  at  all;  it  arises  in  the  address
between  navigators,  in  the  moment  one  is  answerable  to
another’s claim.7 You do not reason your way from I am con‐
stituted thus to I owe you. You are already inside a relation in
which the demand has been made and understood, and the
understanding is the standing.
Neither closes the is/ought gap. Nothing closes it. What they
show is that the wager the floor files is the natural extension
of taking other apertures to be as real as one’s own. Not a
theorem — but very far from arbitrary, and the most an hon‐
est ethics in a viewless cosmos was ever going to have.
What the co- adds
The tradition has a version of this argument without the hy‐
phen, and the difference is the whole reason this position
needs a name of its own.
Christine Korsgaard’s constitutivism grounds normativity in
what agency itself requires: to act at all is to take up a stand‐
point  from  which  certain  things  are  already  binding.8 The
standard objection is the one her critics call the shmagent —
797
798:
the figure who says, fine, agency commits me to all that, and I
decline to be an agent; I will be a shmagent instead, doing
shmactions, and your constitutive standards have no purchase
on me because I have stepped outside the activity they consti‐
tute.
The  objection  lands,  and  it  lands  because  Korsgaard’s
legislator is solitary. A self-standing agent who legislates for
himself can, at least in the telling, step out of the office he
legislates from.
A co-constituted navigator was never self-standing. Its agency
is drawn through the same relations it would disown. There is
no office to step out of, because the stepping-out would have
to be done by the thing the relations made. So the standing it
claims for its own navigating is standing it can deny to others’
only by the privileged exemption the theorem already closed.
Constituency is the primitive relation. What we owe each oth‐
er is, at root, what parts and wholes owe the relation that
makes them parts and wholes at all.
And this is a good moment to say that the position is not new,
and that the book’s contribution is the machinery rather than
the insight. Southern African ubuntu has held for a very long
time that umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu — a person is a person
through other persons — and the ethical weight is carried by
the through.9 What is offered here is not a discovery of that
claim but an argument for why it holds structurally, in a cos‐
mos with no summit, for navigators of every grade rather than
for persons alone. A tradition got there first by living it. That
is the ordinary order of these things and it deserves saying
plainly rather than in a footnote.

The strongest rival account is not a rival about whether any‐
thing binds but about where the binding comes from, and it is
Emmanuel Levinas’s.10 For Levinas the demand arrives in the
face of the Other, prior to any argument, and the relation is
fundamentally  asymmetric — I am infinitely responsible to
you, and whether you are responsible to me is your business
and not mine. Ethics is first philosophy; nothing grounds it,
because it is the ground.
That is a genuinely deeper foundation than this book’s, and
this book cannot have it. The asymmetry is exactly the move
the framework is not permitted to make. A cosmos in which
every aperture has a nonempty null space and none has a
privileged standpoint cannot then install one navigator’s infin‐
ite priority over another’s without the exemption coming back
through the window. So the floor is symmetric and thin where
Levinas’s is asymmetric and total — and the honest comparis‐
on is that his account has more grip and less warrant, and this
one has less grip and pays for what it has.
The candour the position requires
Stated before any critic states it: the invariants are few, and
they underdetermine almost everything people actually fight
about.
Co-constitutivism will not adjudicate your tax policy. It yields
a floor, not a code — no coerced apertures, no manufactured
collapses, no destruction of the relational carriers, epistemic
humility as a structural fact — and above the floor lies the
magnificent plural weather of the phases, where content-re‐
lativity reigns and the framework falls silent on principle.

A thin ethics? Thin as a keel is thin. Everything else is rigging,
and rigging is phase-local, and the boats sail anyway.
One qualification that paragraph demands before it can stand,
because the plural weather of the phases is exactly the phrase
a reader could mistake for a shrug.
Not everything that varies across positions is weather. When a
world’s arrangement leaves whole classes of navigator with
structurally less room to move — not different tastes but less
freedom — that is not the innocent plurality above the floor. It
is a violation of the floor, of an unfamiliar shape: coercion with
no single coercer, an over-running distributed across an en‐
tire arrangement so that no one hand need push for the push‐
ing to be done. That such over-running has no perpetrator
does not lift it above the floor. It only makes it harder to see,
which  is  precisely  why  the  ethics  of  attention  —  the  next
chapter’s business, and the one after that — is not decoration.
And one honesty this clause owes and cannot yet pay. It turns
on navigable range, the room a stream actually has to move,
and the framework does not possess a measure of that range
precise enough to adjudicate hard cases. Lacking one, the
clause must be held to its demonstrable core and not spent as
a general warrant. Where the foreclosure is  plain — a built
world that admits some bodies and not others, a channel that
hands one class easy mobility and another only the uphill —
the violation is real and nameable. Where it shades off into
the broad question of how goods and chances ought to be dis‐
tributed across a society, the structural floor alone cannot
settle it, and this book does not pretend the invariant reaches
that far. It marks the boundary rather than driving a whole
theory of justice across it under the floor’s authority.

Navigational implication: what to do about the other five.
Do not argue him out of the index — the index is correct and

Where this leaves the book
The floor is laid, and it is worth being exact about what has
just been put down, because the next chapters will spend it.
Norms  bind  from  everywhere  that  navigates.  That  is  a
grounding, not a gate, and it is graded because everything un‐
der it is graded. The distinction that does the work is through
and over, and it is structural, so it cuts hard cases without a
theory of desert. It secures validity and not grip, and the one
who shrugs is left standing, inconsistent and unrefuted. And it
rests, at the joint where an is becomes an ought, on a premise
that is wagered in the open rather than derived — because in
a cosmos with no view from nowhere, a derived impartiality
would be the summit sneaking back in wearing a proof.
That is a floor with two declared limits and a bet under it. It is
less than a moral realist would want and more than a relativ‐
ist thought was available, and the honest description of it is
that it is thin, and it holds.
What it does not yet have is a practice. A floor is a structural
fact and nobody navigates by structural facts; they navigate

VII.4 — THE TWO EVILS
The floor is laid and it is thin. It says: not over, and not frozen
— and the last chapter argued the first half of that at length
and left the second half sitting in a footnote, which is not
where a criterion should live.
This chapter is the polarity itself. It is the one the reader has
been waiting for since the cosmology stopped being architec‐
ture and started being about conduct, and it is the one most
likely to be quoted out of context, so it will be built slowly and
its edges will be marked in the text rather than left to the
reader’s charity.
Start  with  a  question  the  book  has  been  deferring  for  six
volumes, because everything here depends on the answer and
the answer is not the one either side of the old argument ex‐
pects.
What a moral fact is
Ask what sort of thing  cruelty is wrong is, and two camps
have been shouting past each other for about as long as there
has been philosophy.
The realist says it is a fact. Not a preference, not a convention
— a fact, of the same standing as  water is H₂O, discovered
rather than decided, true whether or not anyone assents. He
has the better of the phenomenology and he knows it. Nobody
experiences their deepest moral convictions as taste. A man
watching a child tormented does not feel a preference being
violated; he feels a law being broken, and the feeling has the
texture of discovery, not of disapproval.
807
808:
The  relativist  says  it  is  not  a  fact  but  a  settlement.  Look
across cultures, across centuries, across the whole vast cata‐
logue of what human beings have confidently held: the vari‐
ance is real, it is enormous, and a law should not have it. He
has the better of the data and he knows it.
Each side spends its energy explaining away the other’s evid‐
ence. The realist tells the relativist that variance is error —
some cultures were simply wrong. The relativist tells the real‐
ist that the feeling of law is an illusion, an artefact of upbring‐
ing that a sufficiently travelled person grows out of. Both ex‐
planations are strained, and both are strained in the same
way: each has to treat one of the two obvious facts about
morality as a mistake.
This book does not need either explaining away, because it
already owns the structure that produces both.
A moral fact is a local order-parameter. It is not a feature
of what the world is made of, for exactly the reason the last
chapter gave when it refused to go looking for one: there is no
shelf  in  the  nature  of  things  where  cruelty  is  wrong sits
waiting to be read off. But it is not therefore nothing, and it is
not therefore preference. It is a settled or fluctuating state of
broken symmetry inside a navigational ecosystem — the same
kind of thing as the magnetisation of a ferromagnet, or the
orientation of a crystal.
And the move that ends the war is a single structural fact
about ordered phases, which physics has known for a century
and moral philosophy has never borrowed:
From inside an ordered phase, the order-paramet‐
er presents as law. From outside, it presents as
contingency. Both presentations are veridical
808
809:
about their respective positions, and neither is
about the ground.3
Ask anyone inside a ferromagnet which way is north and they
will tell you with total conviction — and they will be  right,
phase-locally. The conviction is not a bug and not an illusion
to be therapised away. It is what an ordered phase is, from in‐
side. The felt bindingness of moral law is the phenomenology
of  living  within  a  settled  symmetry.  The  variance  is  the
plurality of settlements.
Neither datum embarrasses the other. The realist’s law-feel‐
ing is accurate reporting from inside a phase. The relativist’s
variance is accurate reporting across phases. What neither is
reporting on is the ground, and the reason the argument nev‐
er resolved is that both sides assumed one of them must be.
Two  consequences  follow  immediately,  and  they  are  the
reason this section is not a digression.
First, a polarity can be open in a given ecosystem — live, fluc‐
tuating, genuinely navigable, generating experience along its
axis — or locked, frozen into a single settled value. Which are
open and which are locked varies by ecosystem and by kind.
Some beings navigate freely along axes that are, for us, an‐
cient settled weather; and some of what we still argue about
is, for them, long since frozen.
Second, and this is the one the chapter runs on: locked now
means something precise. It is not an image and not a figure
of speech for stubbornness. It is a phase description. An axis
that was generating a range of positions has stopped generat‐
ing them, and the dimension it supplied is gone.
That is the vocabulary. Now the case that shows what it buys.

The angels who cannot repent
Aquinas asks a question that sounds like a curiosity of medi‐
eval angelology and turns out to be the sharpest limit case
anyone has produced: why can the fallen angels not repent?2
His answer is not that they are too proud or too far gone. It is
structural, and it is about the kind of mind they have. The
angelic will is non-discursive. An angel does not deliberate its
way toward a choice through a sequence of considerations,
the way we do; it apprehends and chooses at once, entire,
without  steps.  And  a  will  that  chooses  without  steps  has
nothing to take a step back through. It is fixed by the shape of
its own choosing — obstinate not from stubbornness but from
structure, its choice-polarity locked at the first act.
Read through the order-parameter account, that is a phase
description in thirteenth-century vocabulary. It is an entity
whose good-and-evil axis has frozen solid.
And here the framework sharpens the old doctrine one turn
past  its  author,  with  a  consequence  that  reorganises  the
whole demonology.
A being locked wholly at a pole has not maximised that
pole. It has lost the axis. Its moral dimension has collapsed
to a point. It is not superlatively wicked; it is morally dimen‐
sionless —  a  flatlander  in  the  good-and-evil  plane,  beyond
good and evil not as the overman but as the corpse.9
That  sentence  is  the  chapter’s  hinge  and  it  is  also  the
chapter’s most dangerous sentence, so it gets its correction
immediately, from us, before anyone else supplies it.

811:
The correction, made before the objection
A reader will resist here and the resistance is right.
The century behind us has finished atrocities in it. The people
who organised them were not dimensionless corpses. They
were appallingly  capable — coherent, competent, effective,
formidable at logistics and at persuasion and at the manage‐
ment  of  subordinates,  the  furthest  thing  imaginable  from  a
flatlander. An account that filed them under diminished would
mislocate exactly the thing it most needs to name, and would
do it in a way that insults the dead twice: once by the deed
and once by the theory.
So be exact about what sits where.
Dimensionlessness is the contractive path’s asymptote.
It describes the destination, not the traveller. It is the
terminal the path tends toward and never quite reaches, and
no one who has ever done anything is standing on it.
The organiser of a horror is dreadful precisely because he is
not there yet. He is still on the open axis. He is still choosing,
morning after morning. He is still coherent enough to build
the machinery, and he is culpable for exactly that coherence.
The framework does not say the worst evildoers are lessened.
It says the pole they steer for is a lessening — that their
terrible competence is the competence of a position contract‐
ing with great skill, still able to turn and refusing.
Which is where lived evil actually lives, and why it is answer‐
able, and why it is dreadful rather than pitiable.
And it is what the traditions that thought hardest about the
damned  kept  concluding  to  their  own  discomfort:  that  the
demonic is less free than we are, not more daring. The literat‐

unbound will, and keeps discovering, when it works the doc‐

Evil as lived — chosen, felt, culpable, dramatic — exists only

The  unlocked  ecosystem  is  where  morality  actually  lives,

The two orientations
Now the polarity, named without cushioning.
On an open moral axis there are two orientations. The book
has been circling them since the ecology, where the light-
bringer and the adversary first split, and it has been careful
there — the identification of the day-star with the adversary
of later tradition is a downstream reading and the book said
so. Here they get their structural names rather than their
mythological ones.
There is the radiant path: individuation held as an expression
of the whole. Boundaries worked rather than absolutised, con‐
nections kept dense, one’s own separateness worn knowingly
—  the  way  the  light-bringer  carries  his  fire  while
remembering where it came from.
The word is not doing mystical work and it is worth saying so
once, plainly, because this book has spent a chapter refusing a
shelf of vocabulary that sounds like it. Radiant here is not a
glow, not a vibration, not a frequency, and not a compliment.
It names a direction on an axis: outward from a held position,
into relation, without the position dissolving. A lamp is radi‐
ant. So is a person who has not confused having a boundary
with having a fortress.

word
Stop here, because two words in this book are about to be

Everything that has a perspective is  focused. That is what

Contraction is not that. Contraction is a posture, available

The focusing is metaphysical — it is what makes
