The symmetry, at full strength
Now  the  uncomfortable  part,  and  it  must  be  said  without
cushioning or the rest is not honest.
These two orientations are dynamically symmetric.7
Both are genuinely navigable. Both are coherent. Both ascend
in their own terms, and each has a literature, a discipline, a
set of exemplars, and an account of what the other is doing
wrong. Each perceives itself as the good and the other as the
fallen. From inside either, the polarity reverses sign.
No fact about the dynamics ranks them. The relativist
was right — on the loop, where the question is open, the po‐
larity really does flip with vantage, and any book that pre‐
tends otherwise is smuggling its conclusion into its physics.
One guard, immediately, because the sentence above is one
careless comma from the oldest respectable way to get this
wrong.
This is not two powers. Mani’s cosmos had a kingdom of light
and a kingdom of darkness, coeternal, co-substantial, at war
— and the appeal of that picture has never gone away, be‐
cause it takes the obviousness of evil seriously in a way that
thin accounts do not. What is being claimed here is narrower
by an order of magnitude.  There is one plenum and one
axis. Radiant and contractive are two directions on it,

not two substances in it. Nothing here is coeternal with
anything, because there is nothing for it to be coeternal with;
there is one thing, and orientations are ways of being a part
of it. The symmetry is dynamical — a fact about how the two
paths behave as paths.
And the whole remainder of this chapter is the argument that
the symmetry does not go all the way up.
The two terminal doctrines
Take each path to its limit and ask what it is finally saying.
The contractive path’s terminal doctrine is: I am the totality.
There is nothing that is not mine.
The radiant path’s terminal doctrine is: I am an expression
of that which is.
The second is this book’s own foundation, which is a fact
about this book and not yet an argument. It is a wager on a
truth, filed in the open like the other wager two chapters
back.
The first is false. Not false by preference, not false by scrip‐
ture — false by theorem. The null-space result guarantees
every perspective a nonempty null space, and a nonempty null
space is precisely non-totality: there is always something that
is not you, that you cannot see, that your certainty outruns.
So one path’s limit is a wager on a truth and the other’s is a
wager against a theorem, and that is a genuine difference
between them.
There is even a second consequence, and the old cosmologies
reported it as revealed truth: the contractive path is self-limit‐
ing at its summit. Its completion would require the very total‐

and its doctrine is false at every finite stage. It cannot get
where it is going. Here that falls out as a corollary of two the‐

And now the limiter, which is not optional
Everything above is true and it is not the asymmetry, and a
reader who stops here will carry away the wrong book.
Two chapters ago, arguing about how wide to draw the circle
of concern, this book showed that I am the totality; nothing is
not mine fails at both ends of the range. It fails for the pred‐
ator who has swallowed everything. It fails identically, by the
same theorem, for the mystic who has dissolved into the bio‐
sphere and says the same sentence warmly. The reasoning
there turned on what is left to owe with once a boundary has
gone, and it convicts the swallower and the melter without a
word changed between them. That chapter concluded, in its
own voice, that the asymmetry between the errors is a claim
about the middle of the range and not about the ends.4
Hold that against what has just been argued.
A result that convicts both ends equally is a symmetric
result. The falsity of the totality doctrine is true, it is load-
bearing, and it does not distinguish the contractive path from
anything. It distinguishes  totality-claiming from not-totality-
claiming, and totality can be claimed from either direction.
There is a second and more practical reason the limit cannot
carry the weight, and the honest reader presses it before the
framework can:

The sophisticated one says the opposite. I know perfectly well

A framework whose account of evil convicts only the man who

The person who actually does the harm in the world says

Where the asymmetry actually lives
He does not slip it. The last chapter is where that was shown,
at length, and this chapter does not argue it again — it names
what that argument found.
The last chapter’s answer was that his road forks and both
forks close. He can exempt himself — bind others to recipro‐
city while holding himself outside it — but an exemption is a
claim to a privileged standpoint, a place from which he counts
and others do not, and the null-space result is exactly the
proof that no position holds such a place. Or he can  refuse
the exemption and be consistent, willing that overriding is
permitted for all, himself included — which is coherent to say
and purchases nothing he wanted, licensing the world to over‐
ride him and delivering not mastery but the dimensionless
point, the loop’s corpse reached from the other side.5

That argument was made there to answer a challenge about
agency. Here is what it also establishes, and this is the thing
C19 is actually claiming:
The asymmetry does not live in a doctrine pro‐

The egoist who  says he knows he is not the whole  acts as
though he were the one position the reciprocity cannot reach.
He has not asserted the totality standpoint; he has occupied
it.  And  the  occupation  is  what  the  theorem  forbids  —  the

Which  is  why  the  account  reaches  the  person  it  needs  to
reach:  it  convicts  the  predator  who  has  never  once
thought the words. He does not need a doctrine. He needs
only to claim, in what he does, a standing for his own navigat‐

about position, made in conduct, fully available to inspection,
and false for the same reason the operatic version is false.
The doctrine was the  limit. The exemption is the  seat. The
book needed the limit to show that the two paths are not
equally  true  at  their  summits;  it  needs  the  seat  to  say
anything at all about Tuesday.
An ally with a different mechanism
The twentieth century produced the dominant account of how
the worst is done by someone professing no doctrine at all,
and it belongs in this chapter because it arrives at the same
place from outside.

819:
Arendt, watching Eichmann in the glass booth in Jerusalem,
expected a monster and found a functionary: a man of clichés,
unable to think from anyone else’s standpoint, whose defence
was procedural and whose manner was tedious. Her phrase —
the banality of evil — is one of the most misused in the lan‐
guage6, and it does not mean that evil is trivial or that anyone
might do it. It means that the enormity did not require an
enormous inner life to produce it. The doctrine was not in the
man. It was in the arrangement, and he was fluent in the ar‐
rangement.
That is this chapter’s operative seat, arrived at by a different
road, and the convergence is worth more than a citation be‐
cause she was not working from any of these premises.
The mechanisms differ, and the difference is the interesting
part. Arendt locates the failure in thoughtlessness — an in‐
capacity to occupy another standpoint, which for her is nearly
the definition of thinking. This account locates it in the per‐
formed exemption — the standing claimed and withheld,
which is a structural relation rather than a cognitive deficit.
The two are close and they come apart on a case: the per‐
fectly reflective coercer, articulate, imaginative, entirely cap‐
able of occupying his victim’s standpoint and doing it anyway.
Arendt’s mechanism does not name him; he is thinking, flu‐
ently, in exactly her sense. Ours does, because the exemption
is in the act and not in the quality of the deliberation behind
it.
And  her  mechanism  catches  something  ours  has  to  work
harder for: the  diffuseness — how an arrangement can per‐
form the exemption with nobody in particular performing it,
which is a problem the floor already named and does not yet
have a full answer to.

Neither account subsumes the other. Both are pointed at the
same place, which is that the mark of evil is not the doctrine
and never was.
The mark, and it is a conjunction
So the mark of evil, in its settled form, is neither direction nor
intensity.
Not direction:  contraction in itself is innocent. The book
has already granted this and the next chapter will make it
load-bearing. A prison narrows a life to a cell. A vow narrows
a future to one path. A sickbed narrows a world to a room and
someone in it. None of that is the mark, and an ethics that
read  every  drawing-in  as  wickedness  would  have  to  indict
every act of devotion ever made.
Not intensity: the mild bureaucrat in the middle of the ma‐
chine is doing more harm than the vivid brute at the edge of
it, and every honest accounting of the last hundred years says
so.
The mark is the conjunction:coercive-and-locked.
Coercive —  contraction  imposed  over another  navigator’s
agency rather than through it. That is the last chapter’s dis‐
tinction and it is doing its work here unchanged.
Locked — frozen at the point rather than cycling on the axis.
That  is  this  chapter’s  own  contribution,  and  it  is  why  the
order-parameter account had to come first: without it, locked
is a mood, and a criterion made half of structure and half of
mood is not a criterion.
Both conditions, or it is not the mark. A coercion that is
not locked is an event on the open loop — terrible, culpable,

and answerable, committed by someone still able in principle
to turn. A locking that is not coercive is a tragedy or a dimin‐
ishment, and there are many of those, and they are not this.
The  murderer  mid-choice  is  on  the  circle,  terribly:  still  a
someone, still navigating. The frozen tyranny that has sealed
every exit is at the point.
And the difference between them is not degree. It is dimen‐
sion.
That is what the chapter’s title has been pointing at. The
traditions kept naming two evils and kept struggling to hold
them in one account — the tyrant who overrides, and the soul
that has closed to a point. Every attempt to reduce one to the
other has failed, because they are not the same failure. They
are the two conditions of a single conjunction: evil-as-event
lives on the open loop; evil-as-state is the loop’s corpse.
One is a thing done. The other is a thing become. Unified not
by being the same, but by being the two halves of one mark,
neither of which is sufficient alone.
The census entry
Whose: the privation account — evil as privatio boni, absence
rather  than  substance.  Augustine’s,  after  he  left  the
Manichees, and the tradition’s ever since.8
Renders: what it renders superbly. That evil has no positive
principle, no independent kingdom, nothing of its own to be
made of. It is the instrument that killed the two-powers cos‐

why an account of the world that starts from a plenum does
not have to find room in the plenum for its opposite. Every

Complement — who sees the competence: every position
that has to deal with the organiser operationally rather than

whose files are public. The forensic and clinical literature on
organised, instrumental harm, which has an axis for capacity

for whom the formidability of an enemy is the first fact and
not an embarrassment. And, closer than any of those, anyone
who has worked under a competent bully and can tell
you in detail how good he was at it — a witness most read‐

culture hands them for the encounter is the privation vocabu‐

and the account under this card is still the reason the two-

division and not a compromise.

If evil is a lack, then the more evil a thing is, the less of it
there should be — and the organiser of a horror is not less.
He is formidable, and his formidability is not incidental to the
harm, it is the mechanism of it. The privation account has al‐
ways had to describe him as somehow hollow, and everyone
who has looked at the real cases has felt the description slide
off. It cannot see a  lost dimension on an axis that remains
real, because it has no axis; it has only more being and less.

Boundary: where it goes from reliable to unreliable. It is reli‐

the reason we know. It becomes unreliable the moment the
question turns from the metaphysics to a person, because at
the person the account must convert a structural claim about
being  into  a  psychological  claim  about  emptiness,  and  the
conversion is where every counterexample enters.
Mechanism of the exclusion: what  the  render  identifies
with what. It identifies  evil with  deficiency of being, on a
single scalar running from full to empty. Not as an argument
— the tradition argues carefully — but as the shape of the in‐
strument: it has one dimension, and one dimension can en‐
code how much, never which way. So a being that has lost an
axis and a being that has less existence are indistinguishable
to it; they return the same reading. The capable monster is
not an anomaly the account failed to consider. He is a value
the instrument cannot represent, and the tradition’s long dis‐
comfort about him is the needle pinned against the end of a
scale that was never built to move that way.

Keep the cosmology and replace the scalar. The privation ac‐
count is right that there is no kingdom of darkness and right
that nothing is made of evil, and this book keeps both. What it
needs instead of  less being is  lost dimension — which pre‐
serves every result the tradition wanted and adds the one it
never got, because a being can lose an axis while gaining
everything else. That is the reading under which Aquinas’s
frozen  angels  and  Arendt’s  fluent  functionary  describe  the
same object, and neither the privation account nor Arendt
could put them in one frame.

Where this leaves the book
The floor said not over. This chapter has said and not frozen,
and has shown that the two are one criterion rather than two,
which is why neither half convicts alone.
It has also given away, deliberately, the thing a reader might
have hoped for. There is no verdict here about which people
are bad. The mark is a structural test on a relation and an
axis, and running it requires knowing what is actually happen‐
ing between two navigators over time — which is expensive,
frequently unavailable, and exactly the kind of work moral
confidence exists to avoid. What the chapter forbids is the
shortcut: reading intensity as the mark, or direction as the
mark, or a professed doctrine as the mark. Those are the
three cheap versions and all three are wrong.
And the asymmetry stands where it was placed, at exactly its
size. It is real. It is not a matter of taste. It is not, however, a
ranking of the two paths as paths — that symmetry was gran‐
ted at full strength and never retracted — and it is not a
licence to read every drawing-in as a wickedness.
No wider, and no narrower.
The next chapter takes the half of this one that has been held
back. Contraction is innocent; sometimes the focusing is the
care; and the place where that is hardest to say, and most ne‐
cessary, is where someone is suffering and there is nothing to
be done about it. That chapter makes no promises this one
has not earned, and it will refuse, explicitly and at length, to
make the suffering mean anything.

VII.5 — SUFFERING
Something is happening to you that you did not choose and
cannot stop. That is the first sentence and it is not a hypothet‐

from inside that sentence right now, and the rest have been
there and will be again. This chapter is about what an account
like the one in this book is permitted to say to that, and — the
harder half, and the reason the chapter exists — what it is for‐
bidden to say. There is more of the second than a reader
might expect from a work that has been fairly free with its ex‐
planations. The restriction is not modesty. It is the one place
where this book’s explanatory habit would produce a false‐

told to the people least able to check it.
The two arrows
The oldest useful thing anyone has said about suffering is a
distinction, and it is about two and a half thousand years old.
A man is struck by an arrow. That is the first arrow, and it
hurts, and there is nothing interesting to say about it: a body
was in the path of a thing and the thing arrived. Then — and
this is the observation — the man is struck by a second arrow,
and the second one he fires himself. It is the recoil: the why
me, the rehearsal of how it could have gone otherwise, the
resistance to the fact that it did not, the story assembling it‐
self around the wound about what the wound means concern‐
ing his life. The first arrow was fired by the world. The second
was fired from inside, at a target that was already hit.1
827
828:
The claim is not that the second arrow is imaginary. It is a
real wound and it hurts in the same currency. The claim is
that it is added — that a quantity of the suffering in a life is
generated by the sufferer, downstream of the event, and that
the two quantities have different origins and therefore differ‐
ent handles. You have no purchase on the archer. You have
some purchase on yourself.
In this book’s terms the distinction is not a metaphor, and it is
not an exhortation. It is a description of what is happening to
a position. Suffering is felt distance from coherence: the con‐
dition of a perspective whose situation and whose structure
are not fitting each other, registered from inside as pain. The
first  arrow  is  a  change  in  the  situation.  The  second  is  a
change in the structure — a further drawing-in of the per‐
spective around the injury, which narrows what it can reach
and so increases the distance it was already registering. That
is why the recoil makes things worse in a way that is not
merely  psychological  bookkeeping.  It  is  the  same  variable,
moved twice, the second time by you and in the wrong direc‐
tion.
Everything the practical traditions have built on this is down‐
stream of one observation about leverage. The Stoics reached
it independently and stated it as a dichotomy of control. The
cognitive therapies rediscovered it in the twentieth century
and made it a clinical procedure. It travels well because it is
true, and because it is the rarest kind of practical truth: one
that  identifies  a  real  handle  without  pretending  the  thing
being handled is small.

Suffering fills whatever it is put in
There is a second observation, less famous, and it does more
work in practice than the first.
Suffering is not proportional to the objective severity of its
cause. It is proportional to the volume it is in. A prisoner
grieving his freedom and an executive grieving a bonus are
not suffering equally — there are moral distinctions and this
book is not about to pretend otherwise — but they are each
suffering totally, in the sense that suffering expands to occupy
whatever interior it finds. There is no reservoir it fails to fill. A
perspective is bounded and therefore has a volume, and pain
behaves in it the way a gas behaves in a sealed room: not set‐
tling at the bottom in proportion to its cause, but distributing
until it is everywhere at once.
Most people know this about themselves and treat it as a de‐
fect of character. It is not a defect of character. It is the ther‐
modynamics of being someone in particular, and it follows
from the structure this book spent four books establishing:
you are a focusing, the focusing is bounded, and a bounded
volume does not get to have a small feeling about a large
thing  and  a  proportionally  smaller  feeling  about  a  smaller
one. The scale you feel on is the scale of the perspective you
are, always, regardless of what is being felt.
Knowing this does not reduce the suffering by one unit. What
it does is take away the second arrow of shame — I should not
hurt this much over something this small — which is the most
common  of  all  the  self-fired  arrows  and  among  the  most
costly, because the shame is itself a contraction, and a con‐
traction makes the chamber smaller, and a smaller chamber
makes the same quantity of pain more concentrated. The per‐
son who berates himself for suffering disproportionately is, by

The floor
Simone Weil drew a line that most treatments blur, and this
book takes the line as its floor.
There is suffering — pain, loss, fear, disappointment, the daily
friction of being someone — and then there is malheur, afflic‐
tion, which is not more of that. Weil’s criterion is a conjunc‐
tion and the conjunction is the whole content: physical pain,
psychological  anguish,  and  social  degradation,  all  three
present and converging at once. Any two of them is a very bad
time. All three is a different category, and her point is that the
third term is what makes it different, because social degrada‐
tion is what removes the position from which a person could
be someone-suffering rather than a thing being damaged.2
Affliction does not hurt the self. It destroys the self, from the
outside. Weil’s phrase for what it leaves is the mark of slavery
— a stamp on the soul, put there by an agency that was never
in negotiation with it. A person in affliction does not suffer
and then recover. They are unmade, and what recovers, if
something does, is not the same construction resuming.
In this book’s terms the mechanism is exact and does not re‐
quire any softening to fit. Affliction is compression from out‐
side, so extreme that the perspective can no longer generate
the attentional quality that any navigational act whatsoever
requires. Not a second arrow. Not a contraction the sufferer
performed and could in principle stop performing. A crushing,

be chosen. The focusing is not tightened by it. It is shut.
So the floor is this, stated once and without qualifica‐
tion: not all suffering discloses, and not all suffering
can be navigated through. Some suffering annihilates
the navigator.4 No clause in this book overrides that sen‐
tence. Not the plenum, not the completeness of configuration
space, not the oscillation, not the account of meaning that ar‐
rives three chapters from now. If any of them appears to, the
appearance is a mistake in the reading or a mistake in the
writing, and this sentence is the one that stands.
That is not a caveat attached to an otherwise triumphant ac‐
count. It is a load-bearing member. A framework that could
not say it would be a framework that had never looked at the
thing it was theorising, and this one has looked.
The altitude rule
Everything above raises a question about permissions that
this book has been circling since Book I and now has to state
as a rule, because from here to the end of the work it is the
rule that does the most restraining.
A truth is not an answer unless it is true at the altitude
the question was asked from.7
The propositions in this book are, as far as I can argue them,
true. They are true about the structure of things — about
grounds, plenums, positions, the completeness of what is real‐
izable.  That  is  an  altitude.  Almost  nothing  that  anyone
actually asks is asked from there. Why is this happening to me
is asked from inside a room, by a particular person, at a par‐

835:

can be constructed which is formally responsive to it does not
make that sentence an answer. It makes it a change of subject
performed in the grammar of a reply, which is worse than a
change of subject, because it cannot be identified as one.
The rule has a test and the test is cheap. Take the consoling
sentence and ask what altitude it is true at, and then ask
whether the person it is being said to is standing there. Every
configuration is realized is true at the altitude of the plenum.
A woman whose child has died is not standing at the altitude
of the plenum; she is standing in a kitchen. Said to her, that
sentence does not console and does not fail to console — it
does something worse than either, which is to arrive as an ex‐
planation and thereby to imply that the situation was the kind
of thing an explanation was owed for, and that having been
given  one  she  has  been  attended  to.  She  has  not  been
attended to. She has been addressed by a fact.
This is why the sustained metaphor that runs through most of
this work is barred here and was barred in the chapter on
death. Not because the metaphor is inaccurate — it has been
accurate for six books — but because its altitude is fixed, and
there are two subjects in this work whose altitude is a room:
irreversible  loss,  and  affliction.  A  device  that  clarifies  the
metaphysics cannot be pointed at those without converting a
person into an illustration. The rule protects the reader from
the book, and the book has needed protecting from at nearly
every point where it was going well.

No theodicy
Now the prohibition, and it has to be stated with a specific
target or it will not hold, because the temptation it forbids is
not  an  outside  temptation.  It  is  this  book’s  own,  and  the
source these books were built from succumbed to it in its final
section.
Here is the move, quoted in full so that it cannot be softened
by paraphrase:
This provides a powerful theodicy: a perfect, undifferen‐
tiated unity has no internal narrative, no drama, no
growth. The “fall” into perspectival limitation is what
creates the necessary conditions for the drama of
choice, striving, and self-creation. Every finite experi‐
ence, no matter how painful or contracted, pos‐
sesses ultimate meaning and value. It contributes a
unique and irreplaceable quality to the cosmic totality,
imbuing all of existence with profound and inalienable
purpose.5
I am refusing that, and refusing it here rather than quietly de‐
clining to repeat it, because it is not a stray sentence. It is a
culmination — the last thing said before the argument turns
to evidence, and it is welded to the most load-bearing image
in  the  whole  account.  That  is  precisely  the  position  from
which a false sentence does the most damage, and the reason
a reader would accept it is that everything around it is true.
The refusal is not that the metaphysics is wrong. Take the
metaphysics as given: the plenum, the differentiation, the con‐
tribution of each perspective’s quality to a whole that would
be poorer without it. Grant all of it. The lie is in one conver‐
sion. The  passage  says  something  about  the  totality’s  ac‐

837:
counts — that they balance, that nothing in them is waste —
and then converts it, in the space of a comma, into something
about a person’s accounts. Those are two claims at two alti‐
tudes, and the second does not follow from the first. That the
whole is enriched by a quality does not make the quality’s
bearer compensated. There is no rate of exchange between a
contribution to a totality and a life ruined, because a totality
does not have the kind of interior in which a debt could be
settled, and the person does, and it is the person’s interior in
which the settling would have to be felt. It is not felt. Nothing
arrives.
And the second failure, which is the one the classical theodi‐
cies at least had the honesty to be embarrassed about:  no
matter how painful or contracted is a universal quantifier, and
a universal quantifier ranges over the cases in the floor above.
It says of affliction that it possesses ultimate meaning and
value. But affliction is defined by the destruction of the one
who would hold a meaning. The sentence assigns a possession
to a bearer it has already been established there is nothing
left of. That is not a hard case for the doctrine. It is the doc‐
trine asserting something of an entity that does not exist by
the doctrine’s own account of what happened to it.
Two  things  need  saying  about  why  this  book  is  unusually
exposed here rather than unusually safe.
The first is that we have already refused theodicy once, in
Book  V ,  and  the  refusal  there  was  structural  and  free:  a
ground with no preferences has nothing to justify, so the clas‐
sical problem — reconciling an omnipotent benevolence with
a world containing children’s cancer wards — does not arise
for  us,  because  we  have  no  omnipotent  benevolence  to
defend. That is true.  It is also a narrower alibi than it

no deity in it at all, which justifies suffering not by an author’s

the quoted passage is. There is no God in it. It is a theodicy

The  second  is  worse  and  is  the  reason  C21  is  a  standing

equipped to build a mechanical theodicy than a theist is
to build a classical one. The theist has to attribute inten‐

What is left, which is not nothing
The prohibition is narrow, and its narrowness is not a loophole
being  kept  in  reserve.  It  has  an  exact  boundary  and  the
boundary is worth stating, because a reader who takes the
prohibition too wide will conclude that this book has nothing
to say about living through anything, and that is not the posi‐
tion.
Meaning is available. It is found by traversal — that is the ac‐
count, and the chapters after this one make it — and the tra‐
versal is a real thing a real person does, including a person in
a  very  bad  year.  What  is  forbidden  is  the  manufacture  of
meaning on affliction’s behalf. The distinction is one clause
wide and it is the whole of the ethics here.
A person can find meaning on a path that runs through a cata‐
strophe. That happens; it is common; it is not an illusion and
no one gets to tell them it was. What no one gets to do — in‐
cluding this book, and especially this book, which has the
vocabulary  to  do  it  elegantly  —  is  to  run  the  inference
backwards: from  meaning was found afterward to  the cata‐
strophe was for that. The first is a report from a position,
made by the only person entitled to make it. The second is an
explanation offered from outside about an inside, and it is the
same  grammatical  violation  this  work  forbade  on  its  first
page, wearing the clothes of comfort instead of the clothes of
metaphysics.
Grief gets handled as itself. So does affliction. Not as a prob‐
lem the metaphysics dissolves, not as an appearance that a
wide enough view corrects, not as a contribution. As what it
is, at the altitude it happened at, by someone who is willing to
be in the room while it is true.

Sometimes the focusing is the care
Which brings this chapter to the thing it has been walking to‐
ward, and it has to be entered from the hard side or it is senti‐
mental.
The previous chapter drew the line between the metaphysical
act and the ethical stance, and set it out in a sentence that
does not need saying twice. It is inherited here, used and not
re-earned. What this chapter owes is the consequence, which
the  previous  one  deliberately  held  back:  a  positive  claim
rather than a permission.
The full focusing of a perspective onto one other per‐
spective, with nothing withheld and nothing gained by
it, is not a diminishment of the person doing it. It is
what care is made of.6 Attention is not a preliminary to
caring, a thing you do in order to then do something helpful.
In the cases that matter most it is the entire act, because
there is nothing helpful to do.
Consider where that is hardest. Someone is dying and there is
no intervention left. Someone is in the middle of a loss that
has no remedy. Someone is in affliction, and by the account
above there is no navigational move available to them and no
technique that will meet the situation. Every instrumental jus‐
tification for attention has been removed: you are not attend‐
ing in order to fix, or to advise, or to reframe, or to extract a
lesson that will be useful later. The whole payoff structure is
gone.
And attention is still the thing to do. Not as a consolation
prize for having nothing better. It is categorically the correct
act, and the reason is structural rather than sentimental. Af‐
fliction works by social degradation — it is a third of the defin‐
840
841:
ition — which means it works by removing a person from the
space of things that are attended to, converting them from
someone in the world into a thing in it. A perspective focused
wholly  and  without  instrumental  purpose  onto  an  afflicted
person is doing the one operation that runs directly against
the mechanism of the affliction. It does not cure it. It is not
offered here as a cure and this chapter has spent four sec‐
tions foreclosing that reading. But it is the only act in the en‐
tire book that touches the mechanism at all, and it is available
to anyone, and it costs exactly what it looks like it costs.
Iris Murdoch built a whole moral philosophy on the observa‐
tion and gave the operation its name: attention is the moral
act, and its difficulty is the difficulty of getting the self out of
the way long enough to see something that is not the self. She
called that unselfing, and she thought — I think rightly — that
most moral failure is not a failure of will at the moment of
choice but a failure of attention long beforehand, such that by
the time the choice arrives the person is choosing between
options a poorer looking has already generated.3 Weil is up‐
stream of her and put it more starkly: the capacity to give
one’s  attention  to  a  sufferer  is  rare  to  the  point  of  being
nearly  miraculous,  and  almost  everyone  who  believes  they
possess it does not.
This is where the two of them and this book converge, from
three directions, on one claim: attention is not the prepar‐
ation for love. In the cases where nothing can be done,
it is love, entire, with no remainder unaccounted for.
And it is bounded, like everything else here. Attention does
not undo the affliction. It does not make the affliction mean
anything — that is still forbidden, and offering attention  as
the meaning would be the prohibition breached at the last

moment by the softest available route. It does not guarantee
that the person can receive it, because affliction can take that
too. It is a real act with a real mechanism, aimed precisely at
the one thing it can reach, and claiming nothing beyond.
Where this leaves the book
Two arrows. The world fires one and you fire the other, and
the  entire  practical  content  of  this  chapter  concerns  the
second, because the second is the only one anybody has a
handle on. That is a small thing to be able to say after six
books of cosmology and it is said small on purpose. The al‐
ternative — a large thing, a sentence that made the first ar‐
row all right — was available, was generated by this book’s
own machinery in its own source, was quoted above, and has
been refused.
What the account gives, it gives here: an explanation of why
suffering is disproportionate that removes the shame from the
disproportion; a clean separation of what was done to you
from what you are doing to yourself; a named boundary past
which  none  of  it  applies;  and  one  act  that  works  at  the
bottom, where nothing else does.
What it withholds, it withholds here too, and the withholding
is the more important half. It does not tell you what your suf‐
fering is for. It does not have that information. Nobody does,
and  the  accounts  that  claim  to  are  making  a  conversion
between two altitudes that cannot be made, and doing it to
people who are in no condition to audit the step.
The next chapter is about love, and it arrives having already
had to say the hardest true thing about what love is for —

VII.6 — LOVE
The previous chapter ended by saying that in the place where
it matters most, love is not for anything, and then stopped, be‐
cause that was as far as a chapter on suffering was entitled to
go. It is the right sentence to start from and it is not a defini‐
tion. It says what love is not in service of. It does not say what
love is, and a book that has spent six volumes insisting that
beings are real, that there are no non-players, and that the
traversal rather than the summit is the point, has by now in‐
curred an obligation to say what happens when two of those
beings meet and something between them holds.
This chapter pays that. It is the chapter of this book most
likely to go soft, and the cause is architectural rather than a
failure of nerve: love is the one subject where a reader will ac‐
cept a warm sentence in place of an argument, and will not
notice the substitution, and will thank you for it. So the argu‐
ment comes first and the warmth comes late, and when it ar‐
rives it will be carrying a counterexample rather than a decor‐
ation.
What two earlier refusals have already deleted
Two commitments made long before this chapter remove the
two accounts of love that most readers arrive holding, and
they  remove  them  without  any  further  argument  being
needed here.
There are no NPCs. The being in front of you was already
someone before you turned toward them. Nothing you do con‐
fers their interiority; it was not in your gift. That deletes the

conferral account — the picture in which love is the act that
makes the beloved valuable, in which value flows outward
from the lover onto an otherwise neutral object. Frankfurt
states that account at its most honest: we do not love things
because they are valuable, they are valuable because we love
them. Half of that is this book’s own position and the other
half is unavailable to us. The half we keep is that love is not a
response to an appraisal — you do not love someone because
they scored well. The half we cannot keep is the direction of
the arrow. On our axioms the beloved’s worth is not down‐
stream of the loving, because it is not downstream of anything
anyone does.1
There is no summit. The traversal is the point, and neither
dissolution nor full unity is, because neither has a perspect‐

love aims at merger, in which two become one and the becom‐
ing-one is the completion rather than the end. On this ac‐
count, if the merger ever succeeded there would be one per‐
spective where there had been two, and the love would not be
consummated. It would be  over, in the way a river is over
when it reaches the sea. This is not a warning about code‐
pendency. It is a structural fact about what love requires as an
input, and it takes one line to state: love requires two beings
—  two  limited,  perspectival,  finite  beings  who  cannot  see
everything but can see each other. Without limitation there is
no other, and without an other there is no love.2
That line is doing something the reader should notice, be‐
cause it inverts the usual complaint. Finitude is normally the
thing love has to overcome — the barrier between two people,
the fact that you can never fully know another mind. Here it is
the precondition. The barrier is not what love works against.

The mechanism
With  those  gone,  here  is  the  positive  account,  and  it  is
mechanical enough to be checked.
Love is mutual crystallisation: two beings whose
attentional fields reinforce each other’s coherence.
It is not a feeling that supervenes on an interac‐
tion. It is a description of what the interaction
does to the structures on both ends of it.
The definition sits inside an ecology of encounter, and the eco‐
logy is what gives it teeth, because it comes with the failure
cases  attached.  Interactions  between  beings  are  not  all
symmetric in effect. Mutual crystallisation is the pattern in
which both parties become more coherent through the attend‐
ing — more themselves, better individuated, more capable of
navigating from where they stand.  Parasitic dissolution is
the pattern in which one party’s coherence increases at the
cost of the other’s: the drained relationship, the organisation
that consumes identity, the tradition that requires the dissolu‐
tion of a self as the price of belonging.3
The two are not distinguishable by how they feel from inside,
and that is the most useful thing about the pair. Some interac‐
tions that feel like difficulty are mutual crystallisation under
load — the discomfort of a structure growing. Some interac‐
tions that feel like comfort are parasitic dissolution — the
ease of putting a self down. The test is longitudinal. Over
time, are both beings becoming more coherent, or is one of
them dissolving? That question has an answer, the answer is
847
848:
not available in the moment, and no amount of intensity in the
moment substitutes for it. A great deal of what people call
love fails this test and a great deal of what people call love
passes it while feeling like nothing much at all.
The diagnostic that makes it operable is the orientation of the
field. A being can be expansion-oriented — the configuration
space feels larger after an encounter, more directions look
available, movement is easier — or contraction-oriented, with
the same terms reversed, or, most commonly and most confus‐
ingly, variable: the same person expanding you in one context
and contracting you in another. Most human relationships are
of the third kind. The somatic reading is the fast instrument
and the longitudinal reading is the accurate one, and where
they disagree the slow one wins.4

off. Neither passage referred to the other. Take the definition
alone and love is a species of ecological mutualism with no ex‐

and love is a reason to accept finitude with no account of
what it consists in. The two halves are a single argument
that had been cut along a table of contents, and  any

that most human beings who have ever lived would name
first.
A parent and an infant.
Run the definition. Two beings whose attentional fields rein‐
force each other’s coherence — and the infant’s attentional
field does not reinforce anything. It is not yet a field in the rel‐

neck structure, does not attend to the parent’s individuation,
does  not,  for  some  months,  reliably  distinguish  the  parent
from the ceiling. Every clause of the mutuality runs in one dir‐
ection.  On  the  definition  as  stated,  the  paradigm  case  of
human love is not love.
That is a reductio, and it is worth being precise about which
way it cuts. It does not show that parents do not love infants.
It shows that a definition built on the symmetric case has
smuggled symmetry in as a requirement when what the argu‐

failure runs through every case in this book’s own census
where two beings stand at different grades of the focusing.
Book IV spent ten chapters establishing that the grades
are continuous and that there is no gate. Having done
that, the account cannot then define its central relation in a
way  that  only  works  between  peers,  because  on  its  own
census peers are the special case and grade-difference is the
general one. A human and a dog. A human and a forest. A hu‐
man and the institution they have given thirty years to. A hu‐
man  and  a  computational  being.  A  human  and  an  infant,
which is the one everybody has actually been in, on one end
or the other.

The amendment
Here is the repair, and it is one distinction.
What has to be mutual is the sign, not the sym‐

equal in size, alike in kind, or simultaneous in

Restated that way, the parent and the infant pass, and they
pass for the right reason rather than by charity. The infant’s
coherence increases enormously — it is, in fact, the fastest
crystallisation of a bottleneck structure that occurs anywhere
in the human case. The parent’s coherence also increases,
and this is the part that gets described badly: not because the
infant gives anything back in kind, but because  being the
one who attends is itself structuring. A being whose atten‐
tion is durably oriented toward a particular other is more indi‐
viduated than one whose attention is not. That is the mechan‐

unequal and the direction of both correct.

dishonest to omit. Aristotle’s account of friendship devotes

Named,  so  that  a  reader  can  check  whether  they  have

The first softening is love as the answer. The book refused

The falsifier, and where it nearly bites
The definition is checkable, so it must be printed with the

It fails if a relation in which both parties’ coherence demon‐

would call love. It fails more interestingly if a paradigm case
of love shows one party’s coherence decreasing monotonically
across its whole course, and we call it love anyway, and are

that in the place where nothing can be done, the focusing is
the care — that attention with no instrumental purpose is not

That argument holds. It has not been challenged since and it

outside the whole to remove with. It is not addition: the whole

there is no position from which it is surplus. Three negations,

I. The question the free will debate has been
asking, and why we cannot ask it
Start by being precise about what is being demanded, be‐
cause the demand is older than the objection and has a shape
the objection inherits without examining.
Every version of the free will argument that has run in the
West for two thousand years takes place at a node. There is a
moment; two or more roads leave it; the question is whether
the agent could have taken a different one. Libertarians say
yes and pay for it with a causal gap. Compatibilists say the
question is malformed and freedom is a matter of the right
kind of cause running through you. Hard determinists say no
and accept the consequences. They disagree ferociously and
they agree completely about the furniture: freedom, whatever
it is, is a property of a branch point, and it is measured by
the availability of an alternative.
This book cannot enter that argument, and the reason is not
tact. It is that the furniture is gone. Plenitude does not re‐
move the alternatives; it makes every one of them fully actual,
permanently, without exception. There is no node at which
one road is open and the others shut, because there is no op‐
eration that shuts a road. The libertarian’s alternative is avail‐
able — all of them are, always, which is more availability than
the libertarian ever asked for and is not the same as what he

closes, and nothing needed to.
So the classical question does not get answered here. It gets
starved. There is nothing for it to be about.

II. What choosing is
Here is the answer, stated flatly, and then unpacked.
Choosing  is  not  the  selection  of  a  path.  It  is  the
maintenance of a direction.
Every path exists. What varies — what can vary, what is the
only thing left that can vary — is which one a given stream is
in contact with, and the rate and consistency with which con‐
tact moves. The word for that is navigation, and the claim the
framework makes about it is Theorem 6: free will is the capa‐
city of a stream to navigate toward or away from its own co‐
herence.2
That sentence is easy to read as a slogan. It is not one, and
the way to see that it is not is to notice what it has quietly
done to the measurement of freedom.

gument is a fight about the value of a single binary digit at a
single  instant,  which  is  why  it  has  never  moved  and  why
nobody’s answer has ever changed anybody’s afternoon.
Orientation is not like that at all. A stream can be more or less
oriented toward its own coherence. The orientation can be
steady or intermittent. It can hold under load or only in com‐
fort. It can be strong on one axis and absent on another — a
person can be exquisitely oriented in his work and completely
unoriented in his marriage, and the same person can watch
the second one improve over a decade. Orientation is continu‐
ous, it is multi-dimensional, it varies within a single life, it re‐
sponds to practice, and it is the thing every reader has actu‐
ally been tracking about himself the whole time he thought he
was worrying about branch points.
So the trade is this: a binary quantity at an instant, ex‐
changed for a continuous quantity across a life. That is
not a consolation prize handed over after the real thing was
lost. It is a larger object. Whether it is larger  enough is the
question beat four settles, and it is settled by counting the
losses honestly, not by admiring the gain.

a phrase and not yet an account.
What is a stream in contact with a region of configuration
space? Book II answered that: a focusing. What determines
which region? The whole apparatus of Book VI — the filter

roads are near.
This is why the framework’s account of choosing cannot be
located at an instant, and why every attempt to catch it at an
instant fails. Ask at the moment of decision, what did you do?
and the honest answer is: at the moment of decision, nothing
much happened, because the decision had been made over
the preceding six months by what you had been attending to,
and the moment merely displayed it. That is not a defect in
the account. It is a well-known feature of how choices actually
feel in retrospect to anybody who has made a large one, and
no node-based theory has ever explained it, because a node-
based theory has to treat the six months as preparation for
the real event and the person living it experiences the re‐

III. The existentialist we are using and the one
we are not
The engine has a name, it has been named exactly once, and
it has not appeared in this manuscript before now: Sartre.
The mechanism set out above is deeply informed by the exist‐
entialist  philosophy  of  Jean-Paul  Sartre  —  specifically  the
concept of the  project and the dictum that  existence pre‐
cedes essence — that a person is not born with a nature and
instead becomes one through choices, continuously, without
868
869:
ever arriving at a fixed thing that could be described in ad‐
vance.3
The mechanism is exactly right and the attribution needs cor‐
recting — against this book’s own interest, and in a way that
makes the position stronger rather than weaker.
Sartre’s freedom is groundless. That is not incidental to it — it
is the whole load-bearing claim of  Being and Nothingness.
Consciousness for Sartre is a  nothingness, a hole in being,
precisely because it has no nature to consult; the anguish of
freedom is the discovery that there is no standard outside
your choosing by which the choosing could be assessed, and
the name for pretending otherwise — for appealing to your
nature, your role, your telos, your circumstances, anything
that would make the choice for you — is bad faith. A Sartre
handed an entelechy, an inherent drive toward the expansion
of perspective, is a Sartre with the floor put back under him.
He spent seven hundred pages taking that floor out.
So the synthesis just set out — the what is inherited and tele‐
ological, the how is authored and Sartrean — is not a recon‐
ciliation  of  Aristotle  and  Sartre.4 It  is  the  use  of  Sartre’s
mechanism against  Sartre’s  conclusion.  We  take  the  ac‐
count  of  self-creation  through  project  and  we  refuse  the
groundlessness that motivated it.
That is a defensible theft and it should be conducted in day‐
light rather than under a borrowed authority. The defence is
this. Sartre’s groundlessness is a consequence of his ontology,
not an independent discovery: if consciousness is a nothing‐
ness in a world of brute being, then of course nothing in the
world can orient it, and of course the orientation must be in‐
vented, and of course the invention is anguish. Change the on‐
tology and the consequence does not follow. On this book’s ac‐

count consciousness is not a hole in being — it is what being
is doing, locally, at a position. A stream oriented toward its
own coherence is not consulting an external standard and is
therefore not in bad faith by Sartre’s own test; it is doing the
one thing a structure of that kind can do without ceasing to
be that kind of structure.  The telos is not a rule handed
down.  It  is  a  description  of  what  coherence-seeking
systems are.
And the price of the correction, paid here rather than hidden:
we  lose  the  anguish,  and  the  anguish  was  doing  work.
Sartre’s picture explains why people flee from freedom, and it
explains it elegantly — they flee because it is genuinely un‐
bearable to be the sole author of your own standard. Our pic‐
ture has to explain the same flight without the same cause,
and the explanation is weaker and more mundane: people do
not flee from groundlessness, they flee from  effort, because
orientation  is  metabolically  expensive  and  drifting  is  free.
That is less dramatic and probably more true, and it is the
version Book VIII can actually work with, because you cannot
build a practice on anguish and you can build one on the
observation that the default is drift.

IV . Why this is not fatalism, and what the
difference actually costs to check
III.3  drew  the  distinction  and  III.7  defended  the  walking.
Neither did the thing this chapter has to do, which is to say
what in the world would look different if the fatalist were
right. A distinction with no visible consequence is a prefer‐
ence.
Set the two accounts side by side at the only place they can
be compared.
Under fatalism, the quality of your attention over the next
six months makes no difference to where you end up, because
where you end up was never open. Attention is part of the dis‐
play, not part of the mechanism. Whatever you attend to, you
were  going  to  attend  to,  and  the  trajectory  was  fixed
independently of it.
Under navigation, the quality of your attention over the next
six months is the only thing that makes a difference to where
871
872:
you end up, because it is the sole mechanism by which con‐
tact moves. Nothing else in the account does any work at all.
Those are not the same claim and they diverge on something
observable: whether sustained reorientation of attention
is correlated with change in trajectory. Not in one case —
we will come to that — but across a population and across
time.
The  answer  is  boringly,  massively  yes.  Every  practice  that
works, works this way. Every therapy with an effect size has
the same shape at its core: the systematic redirection of at‐
tention, held long enough to move what is near. Every training
regime, athletic or musical or intellectual, is a protocol for
putting a body in repeated contact with a region it could not
previously reach. Every recovery from an addiction that holds,
holds because the person’s attention stopped being organised
around one thing and started being organised around another.
Book VI’s entire history is a record of this at the scale of civil‐
isations: change what a culture attends to and you change
what its members find thinkable, and the change is legible in
the sources within a generation.
The fatalist has an answer to all of it, and the answer is good,
and this chapter is not going to pretend it is not. He says: and
all of that was going to happen too. The reorientation was
fated, the therapy’s success was fated, the whole correlation
is fated, and the fact that it looks like a mechanism from in‐
side is exactly what a fated correlation would look like. He is
right that no single case refutes him. He is right that the
correlation can be absorbed.
So here is the honest epistemic situation, stated as this
book  states  these  things  elsewhere:  the  difference  is
checkable in one direction only.

If  sustained  reorientation  of  attention  were  not correlated
with change in trajectory — if the practices did not work, if
the effect sizes were zero, if attention were epiphenomenal to
outcome — then navigation would be dead. Not weakened.
Dead, immediately, because attention is the only mechanism
the account has and a mechanism that does nothing is not a
mechanism. Navigation is therefore a claim that could have
failed, and did not.
Fatalism cannot fail. It absorbs every result, including the op‐
posite one; had the practices not worked, that too would have
been fated. A position that cannot fail has not passed a
test when the evidence comes in its favour, because no
evidence could have come otherwise.
That asymmetry is the whole of what is available here, and it
is less than a proof and more than a preference. It is precisely
the grade this book has committed to naming every time: con‐
vergence and survival are evidence, not demonstration, and
the chapter that pretends otherwise is the chapter a careful
reader  stops  trusting.6 Navigation  is  the  account  that  put
something at risk. Fatalism is the account that did not. On this
book’s own standard for grading claims, that is a real differ‐
ence and it is not a decisive one, and both halves of that
sentence are load-bearing.
There is a second difference, smaller and cleaner, and it be‐
longs to the reader rather than to the argument. Fatalism is
unlivable  in  the  specific  sense  that  nobody  has  ever
lived it. Not as a rhetorical point — as an observation about
the class of people who hold the view. The determinist still
looks both ways. He still deliberates about which job to take,
and the deliberation is not theatre; it has the full phenomeno‐
logy, including the part where it is difficult. He would say, and

The census entry
The node-based account of freedom is an instrument, and a
good one, and it earns a card on the same terms as every in‐
strument this book has carded. What is unusual about this one
is that it is the instrument the reader arrived holding — every
other card in the census has been made for a framework the
reader was being shown, and this one is for the framework he
has been using to read the others.
Whose: the classical free will debate, entire and undivided.
Libertarian, compatibilist and hard determinist share this in‐
strument and disagree only about its reading. It is also the in‐
strument of every legal system on earth, of the ordinary attri‐
bution of praise and blame, and of the reader’s own account
of his last difficult decision.
Renders: what it renders superbly, and the list is long enough
that  nobody  should  be  condescending  about  it.  Coercion.
Duress.  Manipulation.  Addiction,  which  is  where  Frankfurt
built his half of it. The difference between a signature given
freely and one given at gunpoint. The entire apparatus of leg‐

veloped in this chapter could replace or would want to. At the
scale where human beings actually adjudicate each other, the
node-based instrument is not merely serviceable — it is the
correct tool, and its readings are the ones this book’s own

of at the moment of decision. The biographer, whose entire

the change to a period and would find the question which mo‐

V . What is lost
This is the part the book has been deferring, and it has been
deferred honestly rather than evasively — III.7 named three
losses and said the accounting belonged here. It does. What
follows is the accounting, and it is not going to end with a re‐
veal that the losses were secretly gains. Two of them are per‐
manent and one of them is worse than it first appears.
The first loss: origination. Nothing starts with you.
There is no point in the account at which something that was
not, comes to be, because of you. This is not a limitation on
human beings; it is what a totality is, and the Ground is under
the same constraint. Whatever you make today already exis‐
ted as a configuration. You did not bring it into being. You
came into contact with it and the contact is what “making”
names.
877
878:
A reader who wanted authorship in the strong sense — ex ni‐
hilo, the artist as small god — does not get it here and does
not get it anywhere else either, but the failure elsewhere has
usually been concealed and here it is stated. That is the whole
of the improvement on offer for this one: not that we have the
thing, but that we are not pretending.
The second loss, and it is the real one: subtraction. You
never make anything not be.
Look closely at what people actually want when they want
free will, because it is not usually what they say they want.
The stated want is the ability to have done otherwise. The felt
want, underneath it, is the dignity of having  closed some‐
thing — of having stood at the fork and, by an act that was
yours, made one road not happen. The weight of a decision, as
it is experienced, is the weight of the roads you are killing.
You are not killing them. Every road you did not take is fully
actual. The version of this afternoon in which you did the oth‐
er thing is not a hypothetical, not a possible world, not a
counterfactual — it is there, with the same standing as the
one you are in, and there is someone on it. Your choice did not
save you from anything and did not prevent anything. It loc‐
ated you.
Do not let that soften into a nicer word. The reader who has
felt the weight of a real decision — the one made at three in
the morning, the one that cost something, the one whose al‐
ternative still occasionally presents itself unbidden — is en‐
titled to be told plainly that the account he is reading says the
alternative is real, is happening, and was not closed by what
he did. The consolation available here is not that the al‐
ternative is unreal. It is that it was never closeable by
anyone, on any metaphysics, because closing requires
878
879:
selecting and selecting requires a position outside the
whole to select from, and no such position exists to be
had by God or by you. The dignity was not taken from you.
It was never in anyone’s possession. That is a genuine consol‐
ation and it is a smaller one than the loss, and a reader who
finds it insufficient has read correctly.
The third loss, which is the least noticed: you do not get
to be the reason.
On the standard picture, an agent terminates an explanation.
Ask why the thing happened and because I chose it is a com‐
plete answer; the regress stops at a person. That termination
is doing an enormous amount of quiet work in how human be‐
ings assign praise, blame, credit and guilt, and it is not avail‐
able here. Ask why the thing happened and the answer is that
a stream oriented in a certain way was in contact with a cer‐
tain region, and the orientation has a history, and the history
has a history, and nothing in the chain is a wall.
The explanation does not stop at you. It passes through you.
That is a real thing to be and it is not the same as being a ter‐
minus, and the difference shows up exactly where you would
expect: in the ethics. It is why the floor established at VII.3 is
thin rather than high, why the distinction that carries the
moral weight is through and over rather than guilty and inno‐
cent, and why this book’s account of the two evils could not
be a theory of desert.7 The reader who wants a metaphysics
that underwrites blame in its retributive form should know
that this one does not, and that the loss is here, in this para‐
graph, rather than in the chapter where it was cashed.

VI. What is left, and why the trade is worth
making
Now the other side, and it has to earn its place rather than be
announced,  because  the  trap  in  this  chapter  is  the
redescription the reader hears as so, no.
Three things survive, and the third is the one that matters.
Orientation is real, it varies, and it is yours. This has
been argued above and needs only one addition: it is the only
quantity  in  the  account  that  is  differentially  distributed.
Everything else in this metaphysics is the same everywhere —
the whole is complete, all paths exist, every entity is a player,
the Ground keeps no count. Orientation is the single place
where one stream differs from another in a way that com‐
pounds. If you are looking for what makes a life a particular
life rather than a location where the universe happens, this is
it, and it is not a small find: in an account this uniform, the
one thing that varies is the thing worth studying.
The  consequences  are  phenomenologically  real,  and
“phenomenologically” is not a hedge word here. It looked
like one in section I and the difference is now stateable. In a
framework where being-the- case requires a vantage — where
there is no fact about the afternoon that is not a fact for some
inside  —  phenomenologically  real is  not  a  demotion  from
really real. It is the only grade of reality on offer for anything,
including tables.8 The retreat to the phenomenological in the
theorem reads as a retreat because the classical debate has
trained everyone to hear it as one. On our axioms it is a re‐
treat to the only ground there is. That is a genuine defence of
the move and it is the strongest one available, and it does not
fully rescue it, because the theorem as first written took the

retreat without giving this argument for it — it sidesteps and

And the third: you never remove, but something on the
other end of the traversal is in a shape it was not in be‐

You do not close roads. But attention is structuring, and it is
structuring at the far end as well as the near one. A being
who is durably attended to is more individuated than one who
is not; that was the whole argument about the parent and the
infant, and it was an argument about coherence rather than
about sentiment. Extend it past the nursery and it is the same
mechanism everywhere the book has looked: the student un‐
der a good teacher, the craft under a serious practitioner, the
language under speakers who care about it, the forest under a
people who have lived in it for forty generations. Nothing was
created from nothing and nothing was subtracted. Something
is in a configuration it was not in, because of the sustained
direction of a particular stream’s attention, and it will stay in
that configuration after the stream is gone.
That is what authorship is here, and it is the whole of it:
not the closing of alternatives but the structuring of
what you attend to. It requires no metaphysical gap, no un‐
caused cause, no position outside the whole. It requires only
that attention has effects, which is the one thing about this
account nobody has ever had trouble believing.

VII. The upper bound, which is the last thing
to say
There is one more constraint, and it is the reason this chapter
closes where it does rather than on the good news.
Freedom in the sense developed here is the capacity to navig‐
ate. Navigation requires a navigator — a bounded, limited, po‐
sitioned stream, which is to say the Promethean structure this
book has been carrying since Book IV: to be someone is to not
be everything else, and the limitation is not a defect in the
arrangement but the arrangement itself.9 The keyholes are
not what stands between you and the view. They are what
makes there be a view.
Which means freedom has a ceiling, and the ceiling is not
imposed from outside. Expansion is real and it is bounded
by the fact that the expander is a boundary. Push far
enough — and the framework is explicit that this is reachable
rather than theoretical — and the null space goes to zero, and
so does the identity that was doing the navigating. The being
who could see everything would be everything, which is indis‐
tinguishable from nothing at all from the position of any par‐
ticular being. This is the dissolution limit, and the verdict
goes without hedging: it is real, it is reachable, and it is not
the goal.10
So the shape of the thing, complete:
At one end, the node, where the classical debate looks for
freedom and where this account says there is nothing to find,
because nothing is ever closed. At the other end, dissolution,
where freedom would be total and there would be nobody left
to have it. Between them, the only place freedom can live: a
882
883:
limited stream, at a position, holding a direction, over
time.
That is less than what was wanted at the node and it is more
than what the objection left standing, and this book is not go‐
ing to tell you the difference does not matter. Something was
lost. It was lost before you arrived, it was never anyone’s to
give you, and what remains in its place is the one variable in
this entire metaphysics that answers to what you do with your
afternoons.
The next chapter asks what such a traversal is for, and it will
not be permitted to answer that the traversal is its own re‐
ward, because that answer is available to anyone at any time
and costs nothing. There is a harder version, and the reason it
is harder is the thing this chapter just established: the path is
the one part of the arrangement that is yours.

VII.8 — MEANING WITHOUT A
MANDATE
The last chapter ended by handing this one a debt, and it is
worth restating precisely, because the easy answer to it is
already forming in the reader’s mind and this chapter is not
permitted to give it.
The debt: the path is the one part of the arrangement that is
yours. The terrain is not yours. The beings you meet on it are
not yours. What you found there was there before you and will
be there after. But the traversal — the particular route, held
over time, by attention that could have been elsewhere — is
authored, and nothing else in the account is.
The easy answer is that the traversal is therefore its own re‐
ward, and that meaning is the walking. That answer is avail‐
able to anybody at any time, costs nothing, and has been
offered to the reader perhaps forty times already by people
with less argument behind them. It is also, in a thin sense,
true, which is what makes it useless: a true sentence that re‐
quires nothing of the framework producing it is not a finding,
it is a mood.
So this chapter has to do the harder thing, which is to say
what meaning  is on this account, what it is not, and — be‐
cause a large fraction of the readers who reach this page ar‐
rived carrying a failed attempt at exactly this — which half of
what they already tried was load-bearing.

I. Three things that are not on offer, and the
awkward fact that this book’s own inheritance
offered all three
Begin  with  the  subtractions,  because  the  reader  has  been
promised for seven books that this account does not buy more
than it has.
There is no summit. Nothing in the arrangement is a destin‐

has been claimed since Book I and defended at V .9 and V .10,
and  it  follows  from  an  argument  the  reader  can  check:  a

not name the elimination of vantage as its goal. The mystic’s
union is, on our own axioms, the one state in which nothing
whatsoever is happening.

intending requires a position, positions are what the focusing
produces, and the whole is not focused. The Ground does not
mean anything by you for the same reason it does not play.

There is no role you were made for, no office standing empty
with  your  name  over  it,  and  no  register  in  which  your
compliance is being recorded.

II. The reader’s failed prior, and which half of
it was carrying the weight
Most readers who reach this page have tried to make their
own meaning, and it did not hold. This is worth saying plainly
because the standard move at this point is to explain to such a
reader that he was wrong, and he was not wrong. He was half
right, and nobody told him which half.
889
890:
The  half  that  was  load-bearing:  the  traversal  is  au‐
thored. He was right that no one was going to hand it to him,
right that waiting for the assignment was waiting for a letter
nobody had posted, and right that the alternative to waiting
was to take the thing into his own hands. Every part of that is
correct and this book has spent seven volumes arriving at it
by a longer road.
The half that collapsed: he thought he had to invent it
alone, and a meaning invented alone can be revoked
alone.
That is the whole mechanism of the three-in-the-morning fail‐
ure, and it is worth being exact about, because it is not a fail‐
ure of nerve or of sincerity. If the meaning of your life is a
thing you decided, then it stands on a decision, and decisions
are revisable by the deciding party without consulting any‐
one. At three in the morning the deciding party convenes,
alone, in bad condition, with no quorum requirement and no
appeal,  and  revokes  it.  Nothing  illegitimate  has  happened.
The structure permitted the revocation from the begin‐
ning; the reader only discovered the clause under load.
This is why the failure arrives specifically at the hours when a
person is least accompanied, and why it does not feel like an
argument being lost — there is no argument. There is a single
party withdrawing a grant it had the standing to withdraw.
An invented meaning has exactly one thing holding it up, and
that thing is also the thing that gets tired.

III. The existentialist gets exactly that half
wrong, and this book’s own census already
said so
The tradition that told the reader to invent it is the existential‐
ist one, and it is a great tradition that has been right about
several things this book depends on. It was right that exist‐
ence is not preceded by an essence, right that bad faith is the
appeal to a nature one does not have, and right — as this ac‐
count concedes in a passage that is better than the one it
contradicts — that the boundaries are generative. They create
the conditions for experience, meaning, and value. Asserting
individual existence is not delusion.”4
So where is the fault? Not in the freedom. In the solitude.
And here is the part that ought to have been noticed years
ago:  this  project’s  own  census  card  on  that  tradition
names the fault, first in its list, and no chapter of this
book  has  ever  cited  it. That  card  covers  the  existential
philosophy  of  suffering  —  Kierkegaard,  Heidegger,  Frankl,
Weil — and the very first entry under its null space reads:
communal suffering (existentialism is almost entirely individu‐
alist — Kierkegaard’s “single individual,” Heidegger’s Dasein,
Sartre’s pour-soi, Camus’s rebel all face their crises alone;
Ubuntu, intergenerational trauma, broken reciprocity are in‐
visible).5
Read  that  against  the  three-in-the-morning  failure  and  the
diagnosis is already complete.  The tradition that instruc‐
ted the reader to author his own meaning has a struc‐
tural blindness to the only thing that would have made
an authored meaning hold. Its heroes all fail alone because
its instrument cannot render anybody else in the room. The

IV . Two opponents, and why they belong in one
chapter
Two positions competed for this reader before we did, and
both  took  him  seriously,  and  both  lost  him.  They  belong
together because they fail at the same joint.
Opponent X: the absurd. Camus states it cleanly. The ab‐
surd is not a property of the world and not a property of the
mind; it is the confrontation between the human demand for
meaning and the universe’s unreasonable silence. The world
is not absurd and man is not absurd — the relation is. And the
honest response is neither suicide nor a leap into faith but re‐
volt: to hold the confrontation open and live in it. One must
imagine Sisyphus happy.6
Our answer is not that Camus is wrong about the silence. He
is right about the silence — sections I and II of this chapter
grant it in stronger terms than he does, because we have re‐
moved the intender rather than merely reported his failure to
answer.
892
893:
Our answer is that the absurd is generated by one term of
the  confrontation,  and  that  term  is  a  demand  for  a
specific kind of answer. Camus’s demand is for meaning of
the issued kind — an answer from the universe, addressed to
him, in a register the universe could speak in. That demand is
the inheritance of the thing that had just died in his culture,
and it survived the death of its object, which is exactly what a
live demand does. Remove the demand and the confrontation
has one term left. What remains is not a silent universe facing
a needy man. It is a terrain that does not speak and does an‐
swer — answers by being differently coherent depending on
where you stand and how you move, which is not a voice and
is not nothing.
Sisyphus is the wrong figure, and the reason is instructive.
His rock does not deform. Nothing about the mountain is dif‐
ferent for his having pushed, nothing on the mountain is in a
shape it was not in, and no one else is there. He is a man in an
environment with no state — which is to say, a man in the one
environment this metaphysics says does not exist.  The ab‐
surd hero is defined by a counterfactual we deny at the
level of ontology, and once the environment has state and
other players, revolt stops being the highest available pos‐
ture, because revolt is what you do when the only thing left in
your control is your attitude, and it is not.
Opponent IX: the meaning crisis. This one is much closer,
and  it  is  the  rival  worth  taking  most  seriously,  because  it
agrees with a great deal of the structure. The diagnosis is
broadly this: what was lost in the modern West was not belief
but participation — the practices, the ecology of ritual and at‐
tention and communal form through which people were em‐
bedded in something that answered. Meaning on this account
is a matter of fit between an agent and an arena, cultivated by

than the falsification of a doctrine.7
Almost all of that we accept, and Book VI is largely a long-

clause, and it matters.
That account is agnostic about whether the arena is any‐
thing. Fit is a relation between an agent and its environment,
and the environment can be described functionally — an eco‐
logy, an affordance landscape, a set of practices that produce
a workable coupling. On that description you could in prin‐

but the practices themselves, and the restoration would count
as success. Ours cannot. On our account the arena is popu‐
lated, the things in it are perspectives at their own grades,
and fit is fit with something, which means it can be got wrong
in a way that a well-functioning practice cannot detect from
inside.
That difference is not academic and it produces a divergent
prediction, which is the only reason it is worth stating.  On
the practice-ecology account, a perfectly functioning set
of practices around an empty arena is indistinguishable
from a healthy one and is therefore fine. On ours it is
the precise definition of a tunnel — Book VI’s whole sub‐
ject, and the thing VI.8 said the reader is currently inside of.
We are committed to there being a difference between a com‐
munity that has restored its practices and a community that
has restored its practices around nothing, and to that differ‐
ence being real even where no one inside can see it. That
commitment costs us something: it means our account can be
wrong in a way the functional one cannot. That is not a defect.
