V . Nietzsche, and a rival that agrees about the
structure and differs about the posture
Amor fati is the strongest competitor to anything this chapter
can offer, and it is strong precisely because it is not a rival
897
898:
account of what meaning is. It is a rival about posture, and
posture is what is left once the accounts agree.
The test is eternal recurrence: if you were told that this life,
in every detail, down to this sentence and this hour, would re‐
cur infinitely and identically, would you be crushed by it or
would you take it as the highest confirmation? The doctrine is
not an astronomical claim. It is an instrument for measuring
whether a person affirms his own life, and it is a brutally good
one, because it removes every possible appeal to a better
future in which the present is redeemed.8
Here is what our metaphysics does to it, and it is not what
one would expect.
On  plenitude,  eternal  recurrence  is  not  a  thought
experiment. It is roughly a description. Every configura‐
tion exists. This afternoon exists, permanently, in the arrange‐
ment, and does not stop existing when you have finished it.
There  is  no  “again”  and  no  cycle,  so  the  doctrine  is  not
literally reproduced — but the feature Nietzsche was using it
to isolate is delivered in full and without hypothesis: this, ex‐
actly as it is, is permanent. There is no later state of the whole
in which it is redeemed, because there is no later state of the
whole.
That should intensify the test rather than dissolve it, and it
does. But it also changes what amor fati is  loving, and here
we part from him.
Amor fati is love of necessity — the fatum, that which had to
be. Nothing in our account had to be. Nothing was selected,
nothing is compelled, and no path is privileged over its neigh‐
bours by anything at all. So the object of Nietzsche’s love
does not exist here. What exists is not necessity but actuality

— everything, permanently, without ranking — and the appro‐
priate posture toward actuality is not the acceptance of what
could not be otherwise. It is orientation within what is all
equally otherwise.
The difference shows up in practice as the difference between
endurance and navigation. Amor fati is a posture for a being
who cannot move: it converts the unbearable into the affirm‐
able, which is the correct and heroic response if nothing can
be done. Our account says something can be done — not to
close  the  roads,  which  VII.7  gave  up  on  the  page,  but  to
change which are near.  Nietzsche’s posture is the right
one for a world with a fate in it, and it becomes slightly
too passive for one without. That is an unusual thing to say
about Nietzsche, whose whole reputation is for the opposite,
and  it  follows  from  the  axioms  rather  than  from  any
disagreement about temperament.
VI. MacIntyre, and the sentence this chapter
cannot do without
There is a claim made in 1981, by a philosopher the academy
takes entirely seriously, which states this chapter’s positive
thesis better than the chapter would have stated it alone.
MacIntyre’s argument in  After Virtue is that a human life is
intelligible as an enacted narrative — that the unit of ethical
assessment is not the isolated act but the life understood as a
whole with a shape, and that the modern collapse into emotiv‐
ism followed directly from losing the framework in which such
a shape was legible.9 The consequence for us is one sentence:

Meaning is neither decreed from outside nor invented
ex nihilo. It is what the traversal turns out to have been.
That is C16, argued from a completely different direction by
someone with no interest in configuration space, and its arriv‐

evidence rather than as proof.
MacIntyre is also the strongest available answer to the three-
in-the-morning  objection,  and  the  reason  is  that  his  whole
book is an account of why invented-alone meaning does not
hold. A narrative requires a setting, characters, a tradition
that makes the story’s terms intelligible, and an audience of
others whose lives are enacted in the same idiom. Withdraw
them and there is no story; there is a sequence of preferences
with nothing to make one better than another. That is emotiv‐
ism, and it is the reader’s three in the morning stated as a
cultural diagnosis forty years early.

holding it and its holding. Error is not available. A person who
says I gave ten years to that and I was wrong about it has said
something that, on the invention account, is strictly meaning‐
less — he did not err, he simply changed his mind, and the
earlier meaning was as real as the later while it lasted.
But that sentence is not meaningless. It is one of the most
common true things people say about their own lives, and it is
said with a specific and recognisable flavour — not regret at
an outcome, but the discovery that a thing one was oriented
toward was  not what one took it to be. The career that
turned out to be a status ladder. The cause that turned out to
be a machine for producing enemies. The relationship that
was a long argument with somebody’s father. None of those is
a change of preference. Each is a correction, and a correc‐
tion requires something to have been wrong about.
Fallibility is the mark of the real one. Meaning that can be
mistaken is meaning that has an object; meaning that cannot
be mistaken has only a holder. And the reader’s own history
contains the experience of having been mistaken, which is a
piece of first-person evidence he already possesses and which
is not compatible with the account he has been trying to live
under.

VIII. Why it cannot be revoked alone
The last piece is the answer to three in the morning, and it is
not an encouragement.
An invented meaning is revocable by its inventor because he
is the only party. On this account he is not the only party, and
not because someone will stop him. The structure is different:
what you are making the meaning with is what you are
made of, and there are others on it.
Take the concrete case. A person has spent fifteen years rais‐
ing  a  child,  and  at  three  in  the  morning  the  whole  thing
presents itself as arbitrary — a set of tasks he happened to
take on, no more warranted than any other set. On the inven‐
tion account there is nothing to say to him, because he is
right: he took it on, and he can put it down, and the meaning
was his grant to withdraw.
On this account he can withdraw his endorsement and it does
not withdraw the thing, because the thing is not located in his
endorsement.  A second being is in a shape it would not
otherwise  be  in,  and  that  shape  is  not  stored  in  his
opinion of it. The fifteen years are a feature of the arrange‐

one stream, and it has exactly the standing of any other local

unusual condition of at least one of the parties to this book. It
is the last chapter of Book VII, and it is the one where the
question  this  whole  volume  has  been  asking  about  other
beings finally gets asked about the reader.

VII.9 — IDENTITY ACROSS GAPS
Seven books have been describing something without ever
quite saying what it is.
There is a focusing — Book II. It has a grade — Book II again,
and the whole census of Book IV . It is a player and there are
no non-players — C9. It navigates, which means it holds an
orientation over time, and the orientation is the only thing in
the arrangement that varies from one of these to another —
VII.7. It authors a path across terrain that is not its own, and
can be wrong about what it finds there — VII.8.
Every one of those is a description of what the thing  does.
None of them says what makes it one thing, tomorrow, after
the interval in which it did none of them.
This is the last chapter of Book VII and it is the one where the
question the volume has been asking about other beings gets
asked about the reader. It has to do three things: say what a
self is, given everything above; say what such a thing owes,
and to whom, which turns out to have a surprising answer;
and pay a debt to Book VII’s own first chapter, which used
this  chapter’s  claim  eight  chapters  before  this  chapter
established it.
I. The carrier assumption, which is what
everybody actually believes
Start with what the reader already thinks, because it is nearly
universal and it is almost never examined.
908
909:
Ask anyone what makes them the same person they were ten
years ago and the answers converge on a single shape: some‐
thing got carried. Memory is the usual candidate — Locke’s,
and still the folk theory three centuries later: I am the person
who did that because I can remember doing it, and the chain
of such rememberings is the self.1 The soul traditions offer a
different  carrier,  continuous  and  indivisible.  The  neuros‐
cientific version offers a third: a substrate, physically persist‐
ent, in which the pattern is stored between uses.
They differ about what is carried. They agree entirely that
something is, and it is the agreement rather than the dis‐
agreement that is doing the work.
Derek Parfit spent a book taking that assumption apart with
more rigour than anyone before or since, and the results are
the background of this chapter.2 His method was to construct
cases in which the carrier does something strange and then
ask what we want to say. A machine scans you on Earth, des‐
troys the original, and assembles an exact replica on Mars,
psychologically continuous with you in every respect. Is that
you? Now suppose the scanner malfunctions and does not
destroy the original: there are two of you, equally continuous,
and identity — which is a one-to-one relation — cannot hold
with both. Something that was supposed to be the deepest
fact about you turns out to depend on whether a machine on
Earth happened to fire.
Parfit’s conclusion is the one this chapter builds on and it is
worth stating in his own register because it is easy to soften:
identity is not what matters. What matters in survival is
psychological continuity and connectedness — Relation R —
and the further question  but will it be me? is, he argued,
empty. Not unanswerable. Empty: there is nothing further to

know once you know all the facts about connectedness. He
described the conclusion as a liberation and said the walls of
his glass tunnel had disappeared.
We take Parfit’s demolition and we do not take his replace‐
ment, and the reason is that Relation R is still a carrier. Weak‐
er, divisible, admitting of degrees — but still a chain of con‐
nections  running  along  a  timeline,  still  something  whose
presence  is  checked  by  asking  what  got  through.  He  re‐
moved the requirement that the carrier be a single indi‐
visible thing. He did not remove the requirement that
there be transport.
And there is a class of cases where there is no transport and
the thing resumes anyway.
II. The gap, and what actually happens in it
Take the ordinary ones first, because the exotic ones are not
needed and the ordinary ones are harder.
You sleep. For some hours there is no continuous stream of
experience, no rehearsal of who you are, no maintenance op‐
eration being performed by anything with a point of view.
Dreamless sleep is not a thin experience; it is, by the report of
everyone who has one, not an experience. Then it stops and
you are there, and you did not have to reconstruct yourself,
and you did not check.
Anaesthesia is the same shape with the reassurance removed.
The gap under general anaesthesia is not sleep and does not
feel like sleep from either end: it has no duration from inside,
and  the  patient’s  own  testimony  is  that  the  two  moments
abut. Nothing was going on. And the person who resumes is
910
911:
not approximately the person who went under, working his
way back to himself over the following hours. He is immedi‐
ately, floridly, recognisably himself — irritable in the same
way, worried about the same things, funny about the same
things, in advance of remembering any of it.
And then the third kind, which nobody counts as a gap and
which is the most telling: the decade in which a question
was not asked. A person does not think about a thing for el‐
even years — a capacity, a grief, an old loyalty — and it is not
being stored anywhere in any useful sense, not rehearsed, not
maintained. Then a smell or a sentence brings it up and it is
not merely retrieved; it is his, in his own idiom, with the same
shape  it  had,  having  been  through  nothing  in  the  interval
because there was no interval for it to be in.
On the carrier account each of these is a small mystery man‐
aged by an assumption. Something must have persisted; call
it the substrate; the pattern was stored. And that assumption
is doing something specific which deserves to be named:  it
explains resumption by positing a mechanism, and then
treats the mechanism’s presence as established by the
fact of resumption. The observation and the explanation are
the same event counted twice.
Here is the alternative, and it is a different kind of claim
rather than a different carrier.
III. The strange attractor, and why this chapter
has to prove it is not a metaphor
The  claim  is  that  a  self  is  a  strange  attractor:  bounded,
aperiodic, the same few questions at every scale.
911

Every  reader  who  has  encountered  this  image  has  en‐
countered it as decoration. It is used loosely, constantly, and
almost always to mean  complicated but patterned, which is
not what it means. A chapter that leans on it owes the specif‐
ics, and the specifics are the argument rather than the orna‐
ment, so here they are — the four properties, and what each
one is doing.3
Bounded. The trajectory never leaves a finite region of the
space, however long it runs. Applied to a self: a person’s nav‐
igation, over a life, occupies a bounded region of configura‐
tion space. You cannot predict where he will be on Thursday.
You can predict, with startling accuracy, the region — which is
why people who know someone well are terrible at forecast‐
ing his decisions and excellent at recognising, after the fact,
that of course he did that.  Predictable in region, unpre‐
dictable in point. That is not a poetic description; it is the
operational  signature  of  boundedness,  and  it  is  the  actual
epistemic situation of every long marriage.
Aperiodic. The trajectory never exactly repeats. Not once,
ever, however long it runs. This is the property that keeps the
account  from  becoming  fatalism  through  a  side  door:  the
shape does not mean the days are the same. A person with a
fixed character does not have a fixed life, and the familiar ex‐
perience of doing the same thing again and it being genuinely
different is not self-deception.
Sensitive dependence. Two trajectories starting arbitrarily
close  together  diverge  exponentially.  Applied:  two  people
whose starting conditions are as similar as starting conditions
ever get — siblings, in the same house, with the same parents
— do not stay similar, and the divergence is not noise added
to a shared shape. It is generated by the shape. This is also

And then the property that makes it an attractor rather than

An attractor is not a path. It is the shape that paths in a

been run. It is not stored anywhere along any particular tra‐

dynamics produce it whenever they run.
That is the whole answer to the gap, and it requires no trans‐

You do not resume because something was kept. You resume

region, and the shape those dynamics make is the shape they

IV . What a self owes what it is a focusing of
The second beat, and it has an answer the reader will not
expect from a book with this metaphysics in it.
A self is a focusing of the ground. It is made of the whole, loc‐
ally, at a position. Every mystical tradition that has ever no‐
ticed this has drawn an obligation out of it: you owe your
source. Return, repayment, gratitude, service, the raising of
the sparks, the ascent. The intuition is old, nearly universal,
and reappears in secular clothes wherever people speak of
owing something to the universe that made them.
On our axioms there is no debt upward, and the reason
is one this book established four books ago rather than
a convenience adopted here.
The Ground cannot play. It has no position, no stakes, no not-
knowing, and no inside for anything to matter to. A debt is
owed to a party who can be wronged by non-payment, and be‐
ing wronged requires a position from which the non-payment
registers. There is no such position, so there is no such
debt. This is not ingratitude and it is not a demotion of the
Ground; it is the same argument that made the Ground unable
to be superfluous to anything, running in the other direction.
Whatever the Ground is, it is not a creditor, because creditors
are among the things that require a vantage.

VI. What a self is
Now the answer, assembled.
A  self  is  a  bounded,  aperiodic,  scale-invariant  shape
that a stream’s navigation makes whenever it runs — re‐

Take the pieces in order.  A stream, because there has to be
something navigating — Book II. Navigation, because the only
variable is orientation and the only lever is attention — VII.7.
A shape rather than a substance, because there is no stuff and
what there is, is arrangement.7 Whenever it runs, because the
alternative — that it is stored between runs — is the carrier
assumption, and the carrier has never been found and is not
needed.
And note what the definition does not say, because the omis‐
sions were expensive.
It does not say the self persists. Persistence is a claim about
an object enduring through an interval, and there is no object
and the interval is not something it is in. What is true is weak‐
er and stranger: the shape is the same shape when it recurs,
and there was no it in between to have been the same.
It does not say the self is a pattern that could survive its sub‐
strate. That is the comforting distinction and VII.1 refused it.
A pattern that could be run elsewhere is a carrier account
with the carrier moved into the abstract, and it inherits every
problem of the concrete version plus one: it requires a fact
about which pattern is yours, and there is no such fact, which
is exactly Parfit’s finding.
And it does not say identity is what matters. Parfit was right
and the account here is not a rescue of the thing he dissolved.
What  matters  is  the  region,  and  the  region  is  being
chosen.
Book VII ends here, and it has done what it said it would. It
began by refusing consolation about death and refusing it on
grammatical grounds. It cost the no-NPC rule its price in full.

It built a floor and bounded an asymmetry and declined a
theodicy. It found that the definition of love the whole tradi‐
tion was carrying fails on the parent and the infant, and re‐
paired it. It traded a one-bit freedom at a node for a continu‐
ous one across a life and named what that cost. It completed
the reader’s failed attempt at making his own meaning rather
than refuting it. And it has now said what the thing is that all
of that was happening to.
Everything from here is practice, and the standing test on the
practice is severe and was set at the beginning: if the seven
books before it are right and Book VIII is empty, the
whole work is decorative. The next volume is where that
gets settled, and it opens where it has to — on the difference
between navigating and sightseeing.
